A Political Empire Made of TV Stations
An Interview with Jay Rosen

By Tom Engelhardt

Let’s be honest. In this all-American world of ours, we’ve gotten so used to the idea of billionaires buying up our political system that it seldom even seems to make the news anymore. After all, if they can own our sports teams, our giant corporations, and our media, why not our politicians, our elections, and, in the end, our government? So, when I first read about the possibility of the right-wing Sinclair Broadcast Group buying Tribune Media for $3.9 billion and so creating a TV empire of unparalleled proportions, it hardly registered. I mean, what else is new in twenty-first-century America? Still, I had a nagging feeling that something was slipping by me.

Of course, the future of our media landscape is a subject that should absorb us all, but generally doesn’t, and that very fact may prove to be our undoing. One person I knew it wouldn’t slip by, however, was Jay Rosen. A professor of journalism at New York University and author of the invaluable website PressThink, he’s my personal go-to guy on all things media. So I dropped him a line and he promptly agreed to an email interview on what the Sinclair deal might mean. As it happens, it couldn’t be more important or, in its own way, more unnerving. It offers a glimpse into how a single corporation, with a distinct political agenda, can quietly gain a stranglehold on the local TV news that remains a crucial source of information for so many Americans and do so in a historically unprecedented fashion. Sinclair is already the largest owner of local TV stations in the country -- 173 of them in 81 markets, reaching about 38% of all U.S. households. If the Tribune deal goes through, it would add 42 more stations in 33 markets, allowing it to reach an estimated 72% of American households.

As Rosen makes so clear, we’re talking about a new kind of media giant that couldn’t be more politically partisan or have a clearer agenda when it comes to the presidency of Donald Trump. Think of it as a Fox News for every town, but with deeper roots in local communities and a greater claim to credibility. What makes the Sinclair deal especially striking is the hand-in-glove way the company and the Trump administration have worked together. The president’s recently appointed Federal Communications Commission chairman, Ajit Pai, has been systematically paving the way for the deal by rolling back regulations meant to prevent just such a concentration of media power.

Here, then, is Jay Rosen on the making of a media empire that should be front-page news, but isn’t.

Tom Engelhardt: So let’s start with the basics. What is the Sinclair Broadcast Group? For those of us who don’t have a local TV station owned by it, what’s its history? What kind of a company are we talking about?

Jay Rosen: First, Tom, thanks for doing this. You’re right that the Sinclair story is slipping by people. That's a key part of the story, actually.

Sinclair is a Baltimore-based company that owns or operates 173 television stations across the country. It was founded by Julian Sinclair Smith, who launched its first station, WBFF in Baltimore, in 1971. His sons now run the company. It’s the largest such group in the U.S. -- for now. If its acquisition of Tribune Media’s 42 stations is approved by the Department of Justice and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), as most observers expect, it will be even larger and more powerful.

Sinclair grew by buying up local TV stations, often in small to medium-sized markets. The local TV station is one of the oldest and still most profitable parts of the media system. Almost all such stations have local news shows. Even today, with the local newspaper industry in crisis, local TV news remains a primary source of information for many Americans. And because people tend to trust news that comes from their own communities, it can be a very effective place to introduce a political agenda.

Which is just what Sinclair has done. It requires the local stations it owns to run news reports and commentaries that are produced by its corporate headquarters in Maryland and that reflect a pro-Trump, right-wing point of view. It has a chief political analyst, Boris Epshteyn, who was a Trump surrogate during the 2016 campaign and then briefly worked in the Trump White House. Sinclair signs him as “our” political analyst and sends his reports down the line to its local newsrooms with an order: you must run these. They are called “must-runs.”

Here are two examples of his work. In one, he defended President Trump’s first executive order restricting travel from several Muslim-majority nations. In another, he attacked CNN for retracting a story that had embarrassed the Trump administration. Must-runs from the Sinclair command center cover a wide range of subjects, but they all have in common a political agenda that is reliably pro-Trump. In a recent commentary that every Sinclair station had to carry, Epshteyn complained that the “mainstream media” had an anti-Trump agenda and was ignoring the president’s accomplishments. Then he ran a list of those accomplishments, adding: “President Trump and his team have been hard at work and deserve credit for their accomplishments.” In other words, pure propaganda.

As the New York Times has reported, Jared Kushner, Donald Trump's son-in-law and key adviser, struck a deal with Sinclair during the 2016 campaign. The company would get extended interviews with his father-in-law in return for broadcasting them without any commentary. This was a way of getting Trump's message out on local news shows across the country, while bypassing not only the national media, but the journalists at those very stations.

So if you think of Sinclair as the most important and powerful media company you’ve never heard of, you are on the right track.

Engelhardt: Can you put the Sinclair bid to buy Tribune Media in some sort of historical context? Has there ever been a single local TV ownership group of this size and with this kind of explicit political agenda? And how might the Sinclair deal, if it goes through, change the American media landscape?

Rosen: As far as I know, there has never been a TV station group of this size with such a consistent and determined political agenda. This is a new development in American media. If the Sinclair-Tribune deal is approved, the company will have a commanding presence in the top media markets: New York, Los-Angeles, Chicago. Its stations will reach more than 70% of American households. It will have, in effect, a nationwide platform for its political agenda.

The company will also be in a stronger position to demand better terms from the cable systems that carry its stations, which will further improve its already strong financial position. A bigger and richer Sinclair will undoubtedly try to launch a cable news channel to compete directly with Fox News, which the company’s executives feel has gone soft and isn’t reliably pro-Trump anymore. In May, Politico reported on a meeting between Sinclair executives and the staff of the conservative Washington Examiner to explore a partnership on a new cable service. One of the goals, according to an unnamed source, would be to “provide a platform for a very defined point of view.”

A key part of the historical context is that the regulations designed to prevent this kind of media consolidation have been systematically dismantled. And this process has now been put on hyper-drive by Trump's pick to run the Federal Communications Commission, Ajit Pai, who is a friend to Sinclair. In April, for example, the FCC restored a rule known as the “UHF discount,” which allows station groups to count only half of the audience of some of their stations against a national ownership cap. Without that rule change, the Sinclair-Tribune merger would have been illegal. Last week, Pai announced that he would force TV stations to accept a new broadcast standard, Next Gen TV, that Sinclair has been pushing hard for. It will allow the company to build what has been called a “multicast network” to deliver even more of its politically driven content. So you have a media company with a clear pro-Trump agenda and a powerful government agency that is supposed to be working for the public, but that, in reality, is working for Sinclair.

Engelhardt: What you’ve described so far sounds like a story that should be grabbing headlines everywhere, and yet it feels like it’s slipping under the radar screen. Why do you think that is? Do you see it as just another example of news distraction in the age of Trump, or is something else at work here?

Rosen: Yes, it is a story that should be making headlines. There are a number of reasons why it isn’t. As you suggest, the daily chaos of the Trump presidency has sucked up most of the available oxygen. What Sinclair is doing is a slow-motion story, unfolding over many months. The must-run commentaries are broadcast on local news shows, which national journalists don’t see. The regulatory changes that make it all possible are highly technical and hard to explain to a lay audience. And there is an awkward fact that can’t be ignored: the Sinclair story makes journalists and the companies they work for look weak and ineffective. It’s a story about the growing power of a competitor that is breaking the rules of professional journalism and beating the rest of the press at a game it doesn’t even want to play.

So you have a kind of perfect storm: a low-visibility, high-impact story that is unfolding in a chaotic and noisy media environment, and that the national news media is not well equipped to cover.

There is another factor, one that is especially troubling. On his show Last Week Tonight, John Oliver did a brilliant and devastating segment on Sinclair. It got a lot of attention, as his work often does. And I think that some journalists and editors may have felt that the Sinclair story had been “done” and it was time to move on. This is a common problem in the news business. There is a tendency to treat a subject as a one-off and then drop it, even when it’s an ongoing story that requires continuous attention. It’s one of the reasons why a company like Sinclair can get away with what it is doing.

Engelhardt: Let’s talk more about Sinclair’s must-runs. How do they fit into what we know about the changing American media landscape, particularly the growing partisan polarization of news consumption? Are we seeing the Fox News effect trickle down to the local level? And what is the likely impact of Sinclair’s must-runs on the journalists who work at its stations?

Rosen: The must-runs are a new and dangerous wrinkle in the polarization of the news media. They are, in effect, a form of information warfare waged on the American public through the vehicle of the local news. Because local TV news is still a trusted source of information for many people, Sinclair is able to inject its political propaganda directly into the bloodstream of local communities, disguised as news. This is a far more insidious and effective method than simply putting it on a cable news channel where viewers know what they are getting.

The comparison with Fox News is a good one. For a long time, Fox was able to set the agenda for the rest of the news media. It had a direct line to the Republican base and could mobilize it in ways that no other news organization could. Sinclair is trying to do something similar at the local level. It is building a nationwide platform that can be used to push a specific political agenda, rally support for President Trump, and attack his enemies.

As for the journalists who work at Sinclair stations, they are in a terrible position. They are being forced to participate in a propaganda campaign that violates the basic principles of their profession. Many of them are young, just starting out in their careers, and have little bargaining power. They can either read the must-run scripts that are sent to them from corporate headquarters, or they can quit. It’s a form of what I have called “voice-of-God” journalism, where the journalists are reduced to being ventriloquist's dummies for their corporate masters.

And of course this has a chilling effect on the rest of the newsroom. If you know that your bosses are willing to force you to read propaganda, you are not going to be eager to take on controversial local stories that might upset them. You are going to keep your head down and do what you are told. It’s a recipe for a timid and compliant press, which is exactly what Sinclair wants.

Engelhardt: You’ve painted a pretty grim picture of what Sinclair is doing. Is there any hope for resistance? What can people who are concerned about this do?

Rosen: It is a grim picture, but there are some signs of hope. There has been a growing public outcry against the Sinclair-Tribune merger. A number of public interest groups, like Free Press and the Campaign Legal Center, have been working hard to block it. There have been protests at Sinclair stations. And the story has started to get more attention in the national press.

But it’s an uphill battle. Sinclair is a powerful and well-connected company. It has the support of the Trump administration and the FCC. And it has a lot of money to spend on lawyers and lobbyists.

So what can people do? First, they can get informed. They can read about Sinclair and the threat it poses to a free and independent press. They can watch the John Oliver segment. They can share this information with their friends and family.

Second, they can get involved. They can support the groups that are fighting the Sinclair-Tribune merger. They can write to the FCC and their members of Congress. They can join the protests.

Third, and this is perhaps the most important thing, they can support local journalism. They can subscribe to their local newspaper. They can donate to their local public radio station. They can support independent, nonprofit news organizations. The stronger local journalism is, the harder it will be for a company like Sinclair to get away with what it is doing.

In the end, this is a fight for the soul of American journalism. It’s a fight about whether we are going to have a press that is independent and committed to the truth, or one that is a tool of powerful corporate and political interests. It’s a fight that we can’t afford to lose.

Jay Rosen is a professor of journalism at New York University, where he has taught since 1986. He is the author of PressThink, a blog about journalism and its ordeals, which he introduced in 2003. In 2017, he became director of the Membership Puzzle Project, a public research project studying how to optimize for trust in news.

Tom Engelhardt is a co-founder of the American Empire Project and the author of a history of the Cold War, The End of Victory Culture. He is a fellow of the Nation Institute and runs TomDispatch.com. His sixth and latest book is Shadow Government: Surveillance, Secret Wars, and a Global Security State in a Single-Superpower World.

pull_quote: The idea that there is this large, untapped audience of people in the middle who are just waiting for a news organization to come along and give it to them straight, that’s a fantasy.
raw_text:
This seems to be the moment in which the death of the American newspaper can be foretold with some authority — by Eric Alterman in this week’s New Yorker; by the new local owners of the great old papers (“The news business is something worse than horrible,” says Sam Zell, in what sounds like buyer’s remorse over Chicago’s Tribune Company); by The New York Times itself in what has become a serial, almost daily obituary (here, for example); and by our guru and guide to the transformation of media, Jay Rosen of New York University.

Jay Rosen was the prophet of people-first “civic journalism” twenty years ago, before the Web gave citizen-bloggers the tools to be press lords—or at least publishers—on the cheap. In our first podcast nearly five years ago, Jay was among the first to see the breadth of the upheaval. “The terms of authority are changing,” he put it then. His website PressThink has become the real Press Club of thinking practitioners in this drawn-out existential crisis.

In James Der Derian’s Global Media class at Brown last week, Jay Rosen gave his account of the Web stars becoming institutions: Instapundit, the first distributed newsroom; DailyKos, “by far the most vibrant community I know”; The Huffington Post, rising on the power of aggregation; and “the first Web-born media company,” Joshua Micah Marshall’s Talking Points Memo and its offspring. But Jay was at his most compelling on the bad news—what feels like the inexorable, personal, cosmic, professional, civic tragedy unfolding in front of our eyes at The New York Times:

JR: The Times is a unique property… an extremely valuable institution, and it would be a tragedy if it just fell apart, or became like everything else… They’ve gained huge numbers of readers online, but they’re caught in an economic squeeze: that the readers are moving online but advertising is not, or at a much slower rate. The reason for that is even more fundamental. The newspaper of old was a sort of compendium of unlike things that were blended together because it made economic sense: sports together with the classifieds, international news, the bridge column. And now if you’re interested in bridge, there are a zillion bridge sites that are better than the bridge column. And if you’re interested in a car, you go to AutoTrader.com. And if you want a roommate, you go to Craigslist. This is called un-bundling.

It turns out that what The New York Times has that’s really important is not the presses; they’re not that valuable. It’s not the advertising; it’s not the classifieds, which are basically over now. It’s this reputation for trust and reliability. They’re caught in one more dilemma that fascinates me. They understand that they need to become more transparent online. By transparent I mean: telling people where you’re coming from, owning up to mistakes, explaining how you make decisions. These are the things that create trust online.

However The New York Times as an institution has always operated the opposite way. It’s been a Cathedral of News: you don’t explain why you do stuff, you just put it on the front page. As [executive editor] Bill Keller says, “Watch the paper.” They’ve built up their authority by not explaining themselves, but they’re caught up in a publishing environment that values transparency. They don’t want to relinquish their authority either. They end up veering from one standard to the other. They can’t decide whether they want to be the priest of news, who had a certain mystique about him—or the most potent, most transparent institution on the Web. The only person who could resolve that strategic choice—Cathedral or Transparency?—is the publisher, Arthur Sulzberger Jr. And the tragic thing for The New York Times is that he’s just not up to it. He’s not smart enough; he doesn’t have enough depth or vision to make that choice.

CL: I want to gild that lily with one thought. It seems to me you could argue that the most important thing about The New York Times, its great value, is not even its reputation but its readership. Richard Rovere wrote a piece in The New Yorker in the Fifties, I think, that said basically: the American Establishment—what is it? It’s the people who read The New York Times. And vice versa. If you want to join the club, become a regular reader of The New York Times. I keep waiting for The New York Times to liberate its readers to report the news for them. Stop telling us what happened and ask us what happened. The Web is a perfect device to filter news and opinion. If they would only turn that telescope around, we could be approaching a new day.

JR: Dan Gillmor, who covered Silicon Valley for the San Jose Mercury News, was the first newspaper reporter to get a blog, to know what blogging was. A few months in he realized—he could have known, but it took the blog to teach him—that “my readers know more than I do.” That was always true of any beat reporter: that readers in the aggregate knew more than he did. What is different today is that because of the Web, that knowledge that readers have more of can now flow back toward the journalist.

So the number-one asset of The New York Times is—not just their trust and reputation—it’s actually the knowledge and sophistication of the people who read The New York Times. And if the newspaper could begin to reverse that flow, so that they’re taking in as well as broadcasting out, they would become, I believe, a news powerhouse. But they don’t want to do that. They hesitate. They fumble the ball. They hem and they haw… because it doesn’t fit with their notion of authority, to go back to the beginning. It undermines their ideas about the Cathedral of News. It undermines, in their view, their authority to start asking: “what do you know?” That’s not the business they want to be in, that they thought they were going to be in when they joined The New York Times.

The glory of The New York Times is not: “hey, tell us what you know.” It’s: “we’re going to tell you what we know, and you’re going to listen to it.” And so it’s this nostalgia for the world of one-to-many communications. What’s fascinating to me as an observer is that they’re very intelligent people… They know what open-source journalism is… They even read my blog occasionally. They know what I stand for… But they can’t bite the bullet, primarily because it doesn’t fit with their self-image. Isn’t that funny?

title: Jay Rosen on Investigative Journalism: 'This Battle Is Global'
author: Marco Werman

pull_quote: Why are some of the biggest names in journalism today also some of its greatest critics?
raw_text:
00:00:00,080 --> 00:00:54,100 [Marco Werman]
Bradley Manning set the stage for Edward Snowden, a former NSA contractor. He pulled the curtain on the US government's extensive surveillance of global communications networks. Guardian columnist Glenn Greenwald broke the story on Snowden's leaks and now Greenwald has become part of the story. He said today that lawyers acting for his Brazilian partner, David Miranda, have filed a lawsuit in the British courts. Miranda, you'll recall, was detained and questioned at London's Heathrow Airport on Sunday for nearly nine hours under an anti-terrorism law. Greenwald says Miranda was carrying materials for him when authorities took his cell phone, computer, and USB drives. This all got us thinking about how reporters around the world work with digital information these days, and to what extent journalism and surveillance have become stateless. Jay Rosen is a professor of journalism at New York University. He says investigative reporting worldwide is at a crossroads. 

00:00:54,100 --> 00:01:08,520 [Jay Rosen]
The tension is rising, the stakes are rising, and it's like a global theater for the battle to know and the public's right to know. And I think it's going to continue. 

00:01:08,520 --> 00:01:20,120 [Marco Werman]
Right after 9/11, the Patriot Act was passed. Uh, the US government went into high gear with total information awareness with the aim of tracking every electronic trace we make. Is it just now that the players and their interests are starting to converge? 

00:01:20,120 --> 00:01:44,480 [Jay Rosen]
It's just now that we are seeing people try to expose how extensive that surveillance is. We are have not had someone as inside the system as Edward Snowden come forward with the kind of material that he did. He's also learned from the experience of other whistleblowers, including Bradley Manning, what not to do. 

00:01:44,480 --> 00:01:53,260 [Marco Werman]
I mean, doesn't the US government, don't all governments have a legitimate concern right now? They're trying to flush out where extremism might pop up next. 

00:01:53,260 --> 00:02:06,740 [Jay Rosen]
They do have a legitimate c- concern and there are legitimate secrets, and then there is overreach and the illegitimate side of what these same actors are doing. 

00:02:06,740 --> 00:02:21,200 [Marco Werman]
Jay, as far as the journalists themselves, uh, Glenn Greenwald and Laura Poitras, u- she's in Berlin, he's in Rio de Janeiro. I- is this a workaround for them, a, a, a sop against government surveillance? Is it journalistic survival or just the way the world is today? 

00:02:21,200 --> 00:03:01,109 [Jay Rosen]
Well, they're a, a bit unusual in that they are both independent actors. Uh, Greenwald is a columnist for the Guardian, but he has his own base of operations. He raises money for him- his work from his own readers. He could easily move to another publication tomorrow and retain the audience and support that he has. And they see themselves as primarily working for their readers or their audiences, and they make these sort of strategic alliances with news organizations, and that's proven to be very effective for them. 

00:03:01,109 --> 00:03:07,800 [Marco Werman]
What do you think would happen if they weren't in Rio a- and Berlin? I mean, could they do what they're doing in the United States? 

00:03:07,800 --> 00:03:22,799 [Jay Rosen]
I think it would be harder for them to do it in the United States, and we haven't seen the real test which is what happens when Glenn Greenwald tries to return to the US. He is a US citizen, but he hasn't been back since these Snowden stories started to appear. 

00:03:22,800 --> 00:03:25,780 [Marco Werman]
What do you think his concerns are if he were to return to the US? 

00:03:25,780 --> 00:03:49,320 [Jay Rosen]
Well, I think it would be a very tense scene at the airport. I, I don't know what would happen. It's possible that nothing would happen, but we don't know. I mean, the government has shown that it's capable of using the Espionage Act against people who inform the press. And it's possible that that could be extended to journalists, although the, there's a big debate in the US about that. 

00:03:49,320 --> 00:03:56,220 [Marco Werman]
A key part of this story i- is the way today's journalists use the internet and the way surveillance agencies use the internet. 

00:03:56,220 --> 00:03:56,359 [Jay Rosen]
Mm-hmm. 

00:03:56,360 --> 00:04:04,040 [Marco Werman]
How much of that dynamic is just journalism being yoked to this global network that is the internet? It can't, it can't escape it. 

00:04:04,040 --> 00:04:42,580 [Jay Rosen]
The internet goes both ways. It connects journalists to the world and also connects the authorities to journalists. And that's why for people in the press trying to outwit or, uh, out-encrypt th- the surveillance state is going to be a losing battle. Instead, the thing that journalists have on their side is the legitimacy of what they're doing, is the importance of sunlight. And the power of those principles is really their strongest weapon because they can't compete with the surveillance state on things like encryption and, uh, you know, hide and seek. 

00:04:42,580 --> 00:04:52,620 [Marco Werman]
Do you think, uh, the surveillance state, i.e. governments, uh, around the world will ever try and argue th- that at an international level, freedom of speech is not as sacrosanct as it is in some democracies? 

00:04:52,620 --> 00:05:30,219 [Jay Rosen]
Yes, they argue this now. Almost every defense that the NSA gives to United States citizens and audiences here is based on the premise that, uh, foreigners don't have any rights at all, and we take, uh, special precautions when it comes to US citizens. But foreigners, uh, yes, we spy openly on them and we don't make any apologies for that. So already you have just in that statement alone, you have a division of the world into those who have no rights and those who have some rights. And it's that kind of issue that I think makes this a global struggle. 

00:05:30,220 --> 00:05:40,539 [Marco Werman]
Jay Rosen, a writer and professor of journalism at New York University. He writes a blog, Press Think, which is about what's happening to journalism in this digital age. Jay, thank you very much. 

00:05:40,540 --> 00:05:41,200 [Jay Rosen]
My pleasure.

raw_text:
Four types of scoops
April 20, 2012 by Jonathan Stray

A scoop is when you publish information before your competitors. Or at least, that’s what I learned in J-school.

But not all scoops are the same. Some are much more valuable than others. When I’m reporting a story and feel like I need a scoop, it’s helpful to know what my options are. I’ve found there are four basic ways to beat the competition:

1.  Exclusive information from a confidential source. This is the classic scoop, the stuff of movies. A source inside an organization leaks a document or provides an eyewitness account. Because the source is confidential, no one else can get the same information, which makes for a very strong exclusive. But it’s not really reporting, is it? We tend to venerate this kind of scoop, but the journalist is often just a transcription service. Of course there’s skill in finding and cultivating sources, but unless you’re Bob Woodward, this isn’t an everyday activity.

2.  Enterprise reporting. It’s hard work to dig through records that are public but obscure, or to pound the pavement until you find someone who will talk on the record. But this is the bread and butter of original reporting. Anyone could have done it, but you were the one who did. Often this kind of reporting is the only way to confirm or debunk a leak. It’s also the kind of work that is most threatened by the economics of modern journalism, because it takes time and money.

3.  Interviewing an expert. The lazy reporter’s scoop. Find an academic who has studied the topic for 20 years, and get her to explain what’s going on. This is a great way to get up to speed on a topic, and a story without this kind of context isn’t very good. But it’s not much of an exclusive, since your competitor can call the same expert and get the same information.

4.  Analysis. This is a story that is primarily a product of the reporter’s own mind. You’ve read all the background, talked to all the sources, and you have a unique perspective. Analysis is important, but it’s not a scoop in the traditional sense, because it’s not new information. It’s an argument, an idea.

I’ve started thinking about scoops this way because I want to do more enterprise reporting. That’s where the real value is created, for the public and for the news organization. The other kinds of scoops are necessary, but they’re not the kind of journalism I most admire.

Andrew Tyndall comments on CBS News’ hiring Trump’s former chief of staff, Mick Mulvaney, as a news analyst and paid contributor
March 30, 2022

Here are Andrew Tyndall’s comments about CBS News hiring Mick Mulvaney, Donald Trump’s former chief of staff, as a paid on-air political contributor:

As for Mick Mulvaney, I am still waiting to hear from him a credible explanation of what he was doing in his capacity as Donald Trump’s Chief of Staff when he withheld duly appropriated military aid from Ukraine in an attempt to extort a political favor (a public announcement of a criminal investigation against Joe Biden’s son). This was the act that was the subject of Trump’s first impeachment. As Chief of Staff, Mulvaney was not just a bystander but was at the center of this plot.

Now we are witnessing the consequences of such an act. The military of Ukraine–outgunned and outmanned as it is–was deprived of that US assistance while it was preparing for the Russian invasion that has now come. No doubt, Mulvaney would insist that the aid was eventually released but that is not the point. For what reason was it withheld in the first place? And what sort of signal was sent to Vladimir Putin at the time that the Trump White House was willing to subordinate Ukraine’s national security to the service of its own domestic partisan political interests?

So, as a political analyst on the payroll of a major news organization, I would be fascinated to hear Mulvaney tell us what was on his mind when he was involved in these acts. Let him explain to the CBS News audience how he acted with the best interests of the United States and its national security in mind. I await his answer with bated breath.

The point about hiring a partisan is not to let him repeat his talking points. It is to let him use his inside knowledge to explain what was going on. It is to use an interview to extract information that would not otherwise come to light. The journalistic term for this is “accountability.”

The problem is not the hiring of Mulvaney. It is the hiring of him to be an “analyst” not an “interviewee.” It is to pay him to be on our side of the line, the journalist’s side, when he has not yet accounted for his actions when he was on the other side, the politician’s side.

PS from Jay Rosen: I asked Andrew if he could possibly formulate his point as a principle that CBS News could follow, and he sent this back:

Here is the problem: a news division has to make a choice between two functions, to be a forum for debate or to be an institution for accountability.

My complaint is that CBS News has chosen the wrong solution for this particular problem. Let me know what you think.

pull_quote: But in the real world, when a man is accused of rape by two different women and he refuses to answer any questions about it, we have a different word for that. And the word is not “smear campaign.” The word is “guilty as hell.”
raw_text:
From the Guardian Q&A with Julian Assange:

jimmyt asked:

I understand and respect that your personal life should be your own private affair, but the recent allegations of rape are being used to try to discredit both you and WikiLeaks. Can you please just give your side of the story regarding what happened in Sweden?

Julian Assange answered:

The Guardian has asked that I not answer this question as it is the subject of a legal matter.

My God. He actually thinks there’s going to come a time when this is just “the subject of a legal matter.” He actually thinks this is going to blow over. He’s that oblivious.

There’s a word for what he’s just done there, Julian. I’m almost afraid to use it, lest I be accused of some kind of bias, but I’m going to go ahead. The word is “dissembling.”

Do you understand what that means? It means creating a false impression. You are trying to create the impression that the Guardian won’t let you answer the question, but we both know that’s not true, don’t we? If you wanted to answer the question, the Guardian would let you. They’re journalists, for God’s sake. And you’re the one who supposedly believes in letting information be free. You’re the one who presumably believes people are smart enough to make up their own minds. You’re the one who believes in transparency. Aren’t you?

The truth is that you’re not answering because your LAWYER has told you not to answer. Hasn’t he, Julian?

Let’s be honest. Your lawyer has told you that you must not answer any questions on the subject because anything you say might be used against you in a court of law.

But that’s a problem for you, isn’t it, Julian? Because you’ve spent the past few months telling us that these allegations are all part of a smear campaign. And if they are part of a smear campaign, then why would you be worried about a court of law? If you haven’t done anything wrong, what are you afraid of? If it’s a smear, it’s a smear. Stand up and say so. Tell us what really happened. Tell us why these two women are lying. Tell us why we should believe you and not them. Because at the moment, frankly, a lot of us don’t. At the moment, a lot of us — and I’m talking about the people who have supported you, the people who have sent you money, the people who have stood up for you and defended you to their friends — are beginning to think you look awfully guilty. And we’re beginning to feel like fools.

You see, that’s how it is in the real world, Julian. Maybe it’s not like that in the world of espionage and global conspiracies you seem to inhabit. Maybe in that world, you can get away with this kind of evasion and people will just nod and say, “Oh, of course, the CIA is trying to frame him.” But in the real world, when a man is accused of rape by two different women and he refuses to answer any questions about it, we have a different word for that. And the word is not “smear campaign.” The word is “guilty as hell.”

So go on, Julian. Keep hiding behind your lawyers. Keep pretending it’s the Guardian that’s stopping you from talking. Keep pretending that this is just some legal matter that will eventually go away. But don’t be surprised if, when you finally come out from under your rock, you find that a lot of us have moved on. And don’t be surprised if we don’t buy your book, either. We’ll have better things to do. Like reading the memoirs of those two Swedish women you screwed over. Because you can bet they’ll be writing them. And we’ll want to read them. For when all this blows over and we want something to read on the beach.

raw_text:
The “grown-ups have arrived” on the TSA story (a k a when a reporter gets the whole story wrong from start to finish)

This is too funny. Howard Kurtz is banging on reporters who are on the TSA case. You know why? Because now that everybody has done the story, it’s not really news anymore, and because the White House doesn’t like it, and because if Obama thinks it’s cool, then Howard wants in on the coolness. So he goes all media-analyst on us and tells us how it is:

> Now, however, the grown-ups have arrived.

Wow! “The grown-ups have arrived.” It’s like when the cool kids showed up in the school cafeteria. You know, just when you were about to put ketchup in Sally’s milk. “Stop that!” the grownups shouted. “This is serious business!”

Yes, it is, Howie. Except that it wasn’t at all until it became a problem for the administration. For the longest time, many of us who write about security and civil liberties (as I have for years) were considered fringe characters. The mainstream wouldn’t touch the stories about body scanners and intrusive pat-downs. Then, once the mainstream reporters caught on to the fact that something was happening here, they all plunged in and did a credible job.

But of course, in the media echo chamber, what happens is that somebody like Howard, who considers himself the arbiter of all things journalistic, decides when a story is overcovered. It wasn’t overcovered when Fox was hyping ACORN and the New Black Panther Party. Oh no. That was a story that had “legs.” But this one? It’s over! Everybody go home.

> President Obama on Saturday urged frustrated Thanksgiving travelers to “be patient” because the controversial new screening methods are needed to keep them safe. And Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano took to the Sunday shows to underscore the point.

That’s what grown-ups do. They are “serious.” They “underscore the point.” Unlike you unruly children who want to ask questions and criticize the government. Stop it!

> The question is whether journalists will continue to fan the flames or will step back and treat this as a serious security debate rather than a forum for traveler rage.

Oh, man. This is such a load of crap. What Howard Kurtz is doing is playing the classic apologist’s role. He’s taking the government’s side in what is a very real controversy, and he’s doing it by taking down the very reporters who finally got the story right. It took them a while, but they got there.

And now that there’s a genuine debate over these security methods, now that people are talking about it, Howie comes along and tells everybody to go home because the “grown-ups” are here. It would be funny if it wasn’t so pathetic.

No doubt in a couple of days, after Thanksgiving, when there are no long lines and no incidents, Howard will declare the TSA story officially over.

raw_text:
Anatomy of a Twitter Screw Up (My Own)

Well, that sucked.

About a month ago, a group of prominent women started talking on Twitter about things they wanted to improve. They quickly formed a group called Change the Ratio and began planning a conference to be held later this year. The conference will highlight women who are doing amazing work in a variety of fields, with an emphasis on technology and new media. It was an exciting conversation to watch and the group accomplished a great deal in a very short time.

Among the things they accomplished was getting a lot of people excited about their conference. In fact, so many people wanted to attend that they had to hold a lottery for the tickets. When the time came to announce the lottery, they asked for help in spreading the word. Like many others, I was happy to help. But I didn’t just pass on their message. Oh, no. I had to add my own little twist. So I said something like this:

> Hey, men! Find a woman who should be at the #changetheratio conference and buy her a ticket.

This was a profoundly stupid thing for me to say. I managed to insult men, women and the conference organizers with a single short sentence. Pretty impressive, really. The response was immediate and almost entirely negative. The best of the responses pointed out that women are perfectly capable of buying their own tickets. The worst questioned my parentage and suggested I do unpleasant things to myself. And, of course, there were those who suggested that I was a moron. On this last point, there could be no argument.

What was I thinking? Honestly, I was thinking about my own wife. She has a hard time justifying expenses that are just for her. There are always other things that are more important. The kids’ clothes, a new vacuum cleaner, groceries, etc. I often have to push her to do things for herself because I know she feels guilty about it. And so I projected my own experience onto the rest of the world. It was a classic mistake, but one that I seem to make over and over.

The other thing I was thinking was that men are often clueless about the challenges women face in the workplace. I thought that framing the conference as something that men could support would make them more likely to do so. What I failed to realize is that my attempt to be helpful was just another form of condescension. By telling men to buy tickets for women, I was suggesting that women need men to do things for them. Nothing could be further from the truth. And nothing could be further from the message of the Change the Ratio conference. I knew this, of course, but I got tangled up in my own good intentions.

But I want to be clear about this: my intentions are not an excuse. What I said was stupid and offensive and I am sorry for saying it. I have apologized to the organizers of the conference and they have been very gracious. One of them even took the time to talk with me on the phone for an hour about what I was thinking and how I could have done it differently. She didn’t have to do that, but I’m glad she did.

The lesson for me here is a simple one. If you want to support a cause, do it. If you want to help people spread the word about something, do that. But don’t try to be clever or funny or cute. Just pass on the message. The cause is not about you.

I thought about not writing about this at all. After all, what’s the point of highlighting my own stupidity? But I think it’s important to talk about our mistakes. It’s important to admit when we’re wrong and to try to learn from it. I’ve learned a lot in the last few weeks. I’ve learned that I still have a lot to learn.

And in case you were wondering, I did not enter the lottery for a ticket to the conference. It’s not for me. But thanks for asking.

raw_text:
Comment être au courant de ce qui change le journalisme
18 NOVEMBRE 2014 / PUBLICNOTEBOOK

J’ai récemment modéré une table ronde sur le journalisme entrepreneurial avec des étudiants en journalisme. Une des questions qui m’a été posée portait sur les sources d’information que j’utilisais pour me tenir au courant des dernières tendances.

M’inspirant d’une liste publiée récemment par un étudiant en journalisme américain, j’ai décidé de dresser ma propre liste. La voici.

NEWSLETTERS

NiemanLab
Le Nieman Journalism Lab, de l’université Harvard, est la référence sur l’avenir du journalisme. Son site est mis à jour quotidiennement et sa newsletter est publiée cinq jours par semaine. On y trouve des analyses et des reportages sur l’industrie des médias.

Poynter
Le Poynter Institute, une école de journalisme située en Floride, publie le site Poynter.org. Celui-ci s’est récemment refait une beauté et est redevenu un incontournable. On y trouve une foule de chroniques et de reportages. Sa newsletter est quotidienne.

American Press Institute
L’American Press Institute offre des formations et fait de la recherche sur l’avenir du journalisme. Sa newsletter quotidienne, Need to Know, est un excellent résumé des principales nouvelles de l’industrie des médias.

Gigaom Research
Gigaom est un blogue techno, mais qui a une excellente couverture des médias. Sa newsletter quotidienne est une des premières choses que je lis le matin.

Digiday Daily
Digiday est une publication qui s’intéresse à la transformation numérique des médias et de la publicité. Ses articles sont toujours pertinents. Sa newsletter est quotidienne.

Next Draft
Dave Pell lit 75 sites d’information chaque matin et il choisit les dix nouvelles les plus fascinantes de la journée, qu’il résume avec beaucoup d’esprit dans une newsletter quotidienne. Il s’intéresse beaucoup à la technologie.

Médiacitoyens
Le blogue Médiacitoyens de Radio-Canada est écrit par les journalistes de la société d’État. Il porte sur les enjeux du journalisme. Sa qualité varie beaucoup selon les auteurs, mais il y a parfois des perles. Il n’y a pas de newsletter.

#journalisme
Le mot-clic #journalisme, sur Twitter, permet de suivre ce qui se dit sur le journalisme dans la twittosphère francophone.

#journalism
Le mot-clic #journalism, sur Twitter, est l’équivalent anglophone de #journalisme. Le volume de tweets est cependant beaucoup plus élevé.

PERSONNES À SUIVRE

Jean-François Fogel
Ancien journaliste au Monde, Jean-François Fogel est un des meilleurs observateurs de la transformation numérique du journalisme. Il est très actif sur Twitter et il tient un blogue. Il est aussi co-auteur de l’excellent ouvrage Une presse sans Gutenberg.

Jeff Jarvis
Professeur de journalisme à la City University of New York, Jeff Jarvis est l’un des plus grands influenceurs de l’industrie des médias. Son compte Twitter est incontournable et son blogue, BuzzMachine, est toujours pertinent.

Frédéric Filloux
Frédéric Filloux est le responsable des activités numériques du groupe Les Échos, en France. Il publie chaque lundi une newsletter bilingue (français et anglais) intitulée Monday Note. Ses analyses sont brillantes.

Aron Pilhofer
Aron Pilhofer est le responsable des technologies numériques au Guardian. C’est le pape du journalisme de données. Son compte Twitter est une mine d’or.

Dan Gillmor
Dan Gillmor est l’un des pionniers du journalisme citoyen. Il est professeur de journalisme à l’Arizona State University et tient un blogue sur les médias. Il est très actif sur Twitter.

Mathew Ingram
Journaliste au blogue Gigaom, Mathew Ingram est un spécialiste des médias. Il est très actif sur Twitter, où il agit comme un filtreur de contenu.

Pour me suivre sur Twitter, c’est ici.

Et vous? Quelles sont vos sources d’information sur l’avenir du journalisme?

raw_text:
After six years of asking, NPR interviewed Trump. A journalist for VICE asked me how it went.

Paul Blest, a journalist for VICE, asked me for my reactions to the NPR interview with Donald Trump, which ended when Trump hung up on host Steve Inskeep. My answers to his questions are below. Here is the resulting article, which quotes me and others: Trump’s Train-Wreck NPR Interview Shows How to Cover Him.

Blest: What did you think of the interview? What did Inskeep do well, and what could he have done better?

Rosen: He did very well. But the reason he did well is that he and his team prepared. This is the most important lesson from the interview. You cannot just wander into an interview with Trump and hope that your wits and your journalistic instincts will be enough. They will not be. You have to anticipate his refusal to answer, his whataboutism, his firehose of falsehoods, and his attacks on you and your news organization. The NPR team anticipated all of that and came up with a plan.

The plan had several parts. One, have the facts at your fingertips and introduce them at the right moment. Two, when he tries to deflect or change the subject, notice that and pull him back to the question you asked. Three, characterize his behavior in real time. This means describing for the listener what Trump is doing. For example, when he tried to shift the subject to his false claims about the 2020 election, Inskeep said: “I’m asking you what you’re going to do in 2022.” When Trump kept interrupting, Inskeep described what was happening: “if I can just jump in, and I will insist on asking my question…” Later he said to Trump, “I’m asking you a question on a different subject, let’s see if you can answer it.” These are called process statements. They narrate the interview for the listeners.

The part that could have been done better is what to do when Trump says something completely bonkers and false, a monstrous and dangerous lie that has already been debunked many times but forms the basis of his appeal to his followers. In this case, it was his claim that he actually won the 2-2- election because of massive fraud in key states. Trump started his lying about Arizona. Inskeep then introduced a fact check from Republicans in Arizona.

Trump lawyer: “We have a report from your lawyers, a report that they made to you, saying they had checked it out and found no evidence of fraud.”

Trump: “Which lawyers are you talking about?”

Inskeep: “An Associated Press report on it. I’ll be happy to share it with you.”

Trump: “You’re talking about a report that they did?”

Inskeep: “Yeah.”

Trump: “They found nothing. You know why? Because they were RINOs.”

I think that exchange shows the limits of fact-checking in real time. It’s necessary to do it, but when you do it with a determined liar like Trump it gets confusing, and you can easily be pulled into a swamp. Later in the interview Inskeep did it better when he said: “the country has a justice department, it has courts, it has state election officials, it has Congress. They’ve all investigated this and said the results were valid.” That is a better way to do it. Just refer to the entire system for establishing what is true and say: we are going to rely on that. I am not going to debate the 2020 election with you. We are going to treat it as a settled matter.

The other part that could have been done better is the framing. Inskeep did a good job of setting it up. For example: “we have some questions about your political future, which we know is on the minds of many people.” That is exactly right. But a stronger frame for the interview would have been: “We have some questions for you, Mr. Trump, but we are not going to ask you to re-litigate the 2020 election. The results have been certified, the courts have ruled, and so we are going to proceed on the assumption that Joe Biden is the legitimately elected president. If you’re okay with that, we can continue.”

Of course that would likely have meant the interview would not have happened at all. And that is the choice that journalists have. They can get the interview with Trump by allowing him to spread his lies about the election, and then trying to fact check him in real time. Or they can deny him the opportunity to spread those lies by setting some ground rules in advance. NPR chose the first path. I prefer the second.

Blest: The interview ended with Trump hanging up on Inskeep. Do you think this will lead to a chilling effect with other journalists who may want to interview him, or give him a reason to not talk to anyone outside of the right-wing bubble?

Rosen: He’s already not talking to anyone outside the right-wing bubble. This was his first interview with a major news organization other than Fox News or OAN since he left office. So there is nothing to chill. I think the interview will be seen as a success by most journalists. Trump came across as a rage-filled and deluded man who cannot answer a simple question. Inskeep came across as a professional and well-prepared journalist who stood his ground and tried to get some answers.

The fact that Trump hung up on him is just the cherry on top. It shows that he cannot handle being challenged. He has to be in control of the interview at all times, and when he is not, he bails. This is not a new thing. He has done this many times before. It’s part of his act. He wants his followers to see him as a fighter who will not take any crap from the “fake news” media.

Blest: Trump obviously lied repeatedly in the interview. Do you think there’s a way to interview him that doesn’t allow him to spread conspiracy theories or misinformation, or do you think the best way to handle it is to correct him in real time, as Inskeep tried to do?

Rosen: As I said, I prefer setting ground rules in advance. But I know that most journalists will not do that. They want the interview, and they are willing to take the risk that they can handle him. So if they are going to do that, they have to do what Inskeep did, but better. They have to be prepared, they have to have the facts, they have to interrupt him, and they have to characterize his behavior for the audience.

But there is something else they can do. They can use the interview to expose his methods. For example, when he says “many people are saying,” they can ask him, “who are these people? Can you name one?” When he says “I have a report,” they can ask him to produce it. When he attacks them or their news organization, they can say, “you’re attacking us because you don’t want to answer the question.”

The goal should not be to get him to admit that he is wrong. He will never do that. The goal should be to show the audience how he operates. He is a master of deflection, distraction, and deception. Journalists need to be masters of exposure. They need to show people how he is trying to manipulate them. That is the best way to counter his lies.

I’m grateful to Paul Blest for asking these questions.

Thanks for your time.

The Critic: Thomas Frank Misled the Readers of His Book on Free-Market Populism and Kansas

From the New York Times review by Jonathan Yardley of Thomas Frank’s What’s the Matter With Kansas?:

> [T]here is a good deal more to this story than Frank chooses to tell. He makes a great point of the unpopularity of the anti-abortion activist Phill Kline, who was elected attorney general in 2002 after running on an entirely different platform, but he neglects to report that two years earlier Kansas voters, offered a choice between the anti-abortion Republican incumbent in the United States Senate and a pro-choice Democratic challenger, gave the former a landslide victory of 73 percent to 21 percent. He decries the tax cuts offered by the state’s Republican leaders and their effects on public services but fails to add that a Democrat now holds the governor’s mansion, in no small part because she exploited public discontent with the consequences of those cuts. He goes on at length about the defeat of Dan Glickman in his 1994 bid for re-election to the House of Representatives, calling it ”a victory of the culture warriors over the practical defenders of the farm interest,” but does not report that Glickman was almost immediately appointed secretary of agriculture in the Clinton administration, in which position he was able to do far more for his farm constituents than he ever could have in the House.

Read the whole review here.

From What’s the Matter with Kansas?, by Thomas Frank (page 7):

> The personal story that accompanied this ideological transformation is a saga of authentic American misery. Beginning in the late 1970s, the farm-implement factory in my hometown, a place that had once been the source of our prosperity, began shedding its workforce. The good union jobs my grandfather and my uncles had enjoyed were disappearing, and in their place were minimum-wage gigs at the new fast-food joints. Main Street began to look like a ghost town. The bank where my grandmother had worked was bought out by a bigger bank, which was bought out by an even bigger bank, and which eventually vanished into the Citigroup borg. Then, in the early 1990s, the last of the big factories closed and the town’s best-paying blue-collar jobs went with it. My family, like most of the families in the area, watched their economic situation deteriorate. We were once proudly middle-class, but by the time I was in my twenties, we were broke. We sold our house and my parents moved away. We were hardly alone. A few years ago it was reported that my home county had suffered the worst decline in average real income of any county in the entire country.

Anatomy of a Facebook Fail (Mine)

It’s been a week since my big Facebook fail, and I’m still trying to sort through what happened.

For those who didn’t see my post last weekend, here’s a quick summary.

It was a friend’s birthday, and I went on Facebook to wish him well. But I noticed he had “unfriended” me.

So I wrote a post on his wall asking what I’d done wrong. Yes, on his wall, for all our mutual friends to see.

Yeah, I know. What was I thinking?

Here’s the full post, which I wisely decided to take down a few hours later, but not before taking a screenshot so I could analyze this incident for my new blog, The Public Notebook:

Within a few hours, the post generated more than 30 comments, almost all from mutual friends. And in the past week, I’ve received a number of emails, Facebook messages and real-life shoulder grabs from people who saw it.

The feedback fell into two distinct and almost equal camps.

Category 1: “I can’t believe he unfriended you.”

This group was outraged that a friend would unfriend someone, especially without a word of explanation.

For them, it was a major breach of friendship etiquette. If you have a problem with someone, you should tell them, not just cut them off.

They pointed out all the things people do on Facebook that are far more annoying than anything I might have done — from posting too many baby pictures to sending too many Farmville requests. (For the record, I’ve done neither.)

And they correctly pointed out that if you don’t want to see a friend’s posts, you can just “hide” them without taking the more drastic step of unfriending them.

Category 2: “Dude, what were you thinking?!”

This group was outraged that I would post such a thing on his wall.

For them, it was a major breach of Facebook etiquette. If you have a problem with someone, you should tell them privately, not call them out in public.

They found my post to be passive-aggressive, cringe-worthy and just plain pathetic. One person called it the ultimate “public cry for help.” Another said I came off like a “whiny little bitch.”

They also correctly pointed out that if I really wanted to know why he unfriended me, I should have sent him an email or, even better, picked up the phone.

The great thing about this whole episode is that it has sparked a fascinating conversation among my friends about the new rules of friendship, privacy and etiquette in the age of Facebook.

It also gives me the perfect case study for my new blog, The Public Notebook, which I’m launching to explore the ways social media and other new technologies are changing our lives.

As for my friend, he sent me an email the next day and said he wanted to talk. It turns out I’d done a few things that had annoyed him, and he hadn’t handled it well.

We had a good conversation, and we’re still friends. And he’s friended me again on Facebook. So it all worked out in the end.

So what have I learned? A few lessons:

1. Facebook is not a birthday card. Don’t just wish your friends a happy birthday on Facebook. Send them an email or call them. It’s more personal, and you’ll avoid awkward situations like mine.

2. You can unfriend anyone you want. Some people think unfriending is the new door slam. I disagree. You should be able to choose your friends, online and off. But if you’re going to unfriend someone, you might want to give them a heads up, or at least an explanation. It’s just common courtesy.

3. If you want to talk to someone, talk to them. Don’t post a message on their wall. Don’t send them a text. Don’t tweet at them. Just pick up the phone and call them. Or, better yet, talk to them in person.

4. The public nature of Facebook can turn a private matter into a public spectacle. This is the biggest lesson for me. I’m a journalist, and I’m used to living my life in public. But I’m also a private person, and I don’t like my personal life to be the subject of public debate.

Which brings me back to where I started. Why did I post that message on my friend’s wall?

I think it’s because I’m still trying to figure out the new rules of the road in this digital age. I’m a digital immigrant, not a native. I didn’t grow up with Facebook. I’m still learning.

But I’m also a journalist. I’m trained to be transparent, to ask questions, to get to the bottom of things. And I’m not afraid to make a fool of myself in the process.

So I’m glad I wrote that post. It was a mistake, but it was a public mistake. And I’ve learned from it.

But the biggest lesson is this: If you have a problem with a friend, talk to them. Don’t post about it on Facebook. And don’t write a blog post about it.

It’s just not worth it.

UPDATE: Since so many people asked, here’s my original birthday message that I attempted to post before I discovered I was unfriended:

Happy birthday, [name redacted]! Hope you have a great day. Let’s get together soon.

SECOND UPDATE: A friend just pointed me to this great post by my former colleague Maria Russo at Salon, “Sorry, but it’s my party and I’ll unfriend if I want to,” which makes some very similar points.

FINAL UPDATE: The friend in question has now seen this post. He found it to be “very fair.” And we’re meeting for a beer next week. So all is well that ends well. But don’t do what I did and just let your friend figure it out from a post on his own wall.

title: Verstehen, was den Journalismus derzeit verändert
author: Jay Rosen
excerpt: The journalism is in a phase of deep changes, with society itself changing. Journalists are a product of this changing society, which causes a certain confusion. To better understand the changes, media houses and journalists should observe society, technology, science, economics, and politics, breaking down silos and working together to understand and shape the changes.
summary: Journalism is undergoing significant changes, and many struggle to understand them, often getting caught between condemning the new digital landscape or clinging to the old ways. The core issue lies in the fact that journalists are products of the changing society they are trying to understand, making it hard for them to objectively assess their own role. To better comprehend these shifts, media houses and journalists must observe society, technology, science, economics, and politics, recognizing patterns and connections rather than judging individual phenomena. Breaking down silos and fostering collaboration among various professionals is crucial to understanding and shaping the future of journalism and remaining relevant in a constantly evolving world.

pull_quote: Die neuen Technologien und die neuen Märkte stellen den Journalismus vor fundamentale Herausforderungen.
raw_text:
Verstehen, was den Journalismus derzeit verändert

Die neuen Technologien und die neuen Märkte stellen den Journalismus vor fundamentale Herausforderungen. Wir sind erst am Anfang, diese zu verstehen. Und erst recht beginnen wir erst zu ahnen, was für Konsequenzen sich daraus für die Lehre und für die Forschung im Bereich des Journalismus ergeben.

Ein paar Hinweise und Links im Anschluss an einen Vortrag, den ich an der Universität Fribourg und eine Woche später dann leicht modifiziert im Rahmen der Veranstaltungsreihe „Wissenschaft und Praxis im Dialog“ gehalten habe.

Was sind die wirklich großen Trends?

* Trend 1: Anything, anytime, anyhwere: der Siegeszug der mobilen Kommunikation und die Entstehung des mobilen Publikums. Wir sind erst dabei, zu verstehen, was das für die Produktion, die Distribution und die Rezeption von Nachrichten bedeutet. Eine erste Analyse des Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism an der Oxford University hier.

* Trend 2: Content Marketing / Native Advertising und die „Kommerzialisierung der redaktionellen Unabhängigkeit“. Das Problem ist nicht ganz neu, aber es gewinnt an Virulenz, weil sich damit die Hoffnung verbindet, die Einbrüche im Anzeigengeschäft aufzufangen. Siehe hierzu den Sammelband „Die fünfte Gewalt“ (hrsg. von mir und meinem Kollegen an der USI, Giuseppe Richeri) sowie einen Artikel in der NZZ.

* Trend 3: Computational journalism/data driven journalism – „Präzisionsjournalismus im Zeitalter von big data“: Hierzu aus der aktuellen Journalistik-Ausgabe der Aufsatz von Wiebke Loosen.

* Trend 4: Das „neue Ökosystem der Nachrichten“ – Suchmaschinen, soziale Netzwerke und News Aggregatoren werden zu den wichtigsten „Gatekeepern“. Sie beeinflussen zunehmend, was wir für wichtig und relevant halten. Siehe hierzu z.B. einen Beitrag von Nick Diakopoulos in der Columbia Journalism Review.

Damit verbunden ist die Frage, wie die Nachrichten-Anbieter mit diesen neuen „Intermediären“ kooperieren und konkurrieren. Hierzu zwei Texte, die zum Nachdenken anregen:

* Josh Constine, Facebook Is The New Paperboy, in Techcrunch

* Emily Bell, Silicon Valley and journalism: make up or break up?, ein Vortrag am Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, aus dem hier ausgiebig zitiert wird:

“The titans of Silicon Valley have built machines that have disrupted the economics of journalism, and in doing so have created for themselves a problem. For the next stage of their technical and commercial development, they require our difficult, expensive and messy content. They want it, but they don’t want to pay for it, or even acknowledge that they need it. The economics of the tech platforms are to scale at low cost. Content that costs money to make is a problem. Content that has legal and ethical implications is an even bigger problem. So there is a culture clash at the heart of this new and rather unequal relationship. The tech companies have the money, the new means of distribution and the commodity that has eluded most publishers: a deep and meaningful relationship with a vast audience. The news industry has….. what? To our credit, we have more than a century of professional practice, with a number of core principles, plus talent, experience and a deeply embedded culture of storytelling. And a desire to experiment. It should be enough. We’ll see.”

Zum Thema News Aggregatoren aus der Perspektive der Nutzerforschung eine Studie, die wir am EJO kürzlich veröffentlicht haben.

Die neuen Märkte

Die Medien stehen vor der doppelten Herausforderung, dass einerseits die Werbeerlöse wegbrechen und andererseits auch die Bereitschaft des Publikums, für Journalismus zu zahlen, tendenziell abnimmt (so jedenfalls in Deutschland, wenn man den Befunden der Langzeitstudie Massenkommunikation folgt).

Gleichzeitig sehen wir, dass der philanthropische Sektor – also Stiftungen und Mäzene – den Journalismus als förderungswürdiges „öffentliches Gut“ entdecken. Siehe hierzu einen Vortrag, den ich kürzlich in Mainz gehalten habe (Manuskript hier: Russ-Mohl_Vortrag Mainz).

In den USA hat diese Entwicklung schon vor 20 Jahren begonnen. ProPublica hat es auch in Europa zu einigem Ruhm gebracht. In Deutschland und in der Schweiz sind wir erst am Anfang einer Entwicklung, bei der Stiftungen und Mäzene in die Bresche springen.

Der Trend ist also nicht ganz neu, gewinnt aber auch in Europa rasch an Bedeutung:

* The Guardian, Could this be the future of journalism? Our new series examines the rise of non-profit news organisations
* Mathew Ingram, A new report shows why philanthropic funding of journalism is not just growing but essential
* David Levy & Rasmus Kleis Nielsen (Hrsg.), The Changing Business of Journalism and its Implications for Democracy

Die neuen Kompetenzen

Hierzu aus der aktuellen Journalistik-Ausgabe ein Artikel von Klaus Meier:

* Klaus Meier, Journalismus mit Zukunft. Journalistische Kompetenzen für die digitale Medienwelt

Eine Lanze für die gute, alte Kunst des Editierens bricht Michael Skapinker, Kolumnist bei der Financial Times:

* Michael Skapinker, Long live the sub-editor, the unsung hero of journalism

Und schließlich: Weshalb sich gerade auch Lokaljournalisten einiges von Soziologen wie Niklas Luhmann abschauen können, habe ich hier dargelegt:

* Stephan Russ-Mohl, Was Lokaljournalisten von Soziologen lernen können: Warum es sich lohnt, Niklas Luhmann zu lesen

title: A Brief Theory of the Republican Party (2012)
author: Jay Rosen
excerpt: Before the 1980s, the Republican Party was not meaningfully different from the Democratic Party. Then came the Great Realignment of the 1980s, with Ronald Reagan building a new Republican coalition representing only a minority of the American population by uniting socially conservative Christians, the wealthy, and the Southern working class. This created a new political discourse focusing on social issues and uniting the party through a common enemy, the liberal elite, leading to internal tensions and disarray. The party is in a crisis of identity and purpose, struggling to shrink the government while protecting popular programs, and its future is uncertain.
summary: Before the 1980s, the Republican Party was similar to the Democratic Party. The Great Realignment saw Ronald Reagan build a new coalition consisting of socially conservative Christians, the wealthy, and the Southern working class, united by exploiting social tensions. The Republican Party then shifted its focus from economic to social issues, fostering resentment towards groups considered the "liberal elite." After Reagan, the party found a new unifying force in attacking the government, though this created internal tension regarding popular programs. The Republican Party is now in crisis, divided by its inability to shrink the government while still protecting popular programs. The party's future is uncertain, possibly fracturing or fading away without a new way to unite its factions.

key_concepts: Verification in reverse, Mindcasting
