pull_quote: The party is going to have to decide whether its future lies with the evangelical Christians of the heartland or with the secular, pro-business voters of the suburbs. It cannot be the party of both Rick Santorum and Mitt Romney. It has to choose.
raw_text:
A Brief Theory of the Republican Party, 2012

The 2012 Republican Primary season has been nothing if not entertaining. At various points, we have had no fewer than five candidates who have been touted by one media source or another as the ‘frontrunner’ for the nomination. First there was Michelle Bachmann, who imploded spectacularly after winning the Iowa straw poll. Then there was Rick Perry, who will be remembered for little else other than his magnificent ‘oops’ moment in a televised debate. Then there was the brief, but glorious, ascendancy of Herman Cain, who was ultimately brought down by a combination of his own vacuity and a series of lurid accusations. Now there is Newt Gingrich, the thrice-married former speaker of the House who has recently shot up in the polls, only to be hammered back down by a series of devastating attack ads funded by his main rival.

And then there is Mitt Romney. The man who has been the most consistent frontrunner (insofar as it is possible to be a consistent frontrunner in this race), but who seems unable to seal the deal with the Republican base. Romney is the man that the Republican establishment wants to win. He is a mainstream, pro-business candidate who has executive experience (as Governor of Massachusetts) and who does not have a history of making embarrassing gaffes. However, he is also distrusted by the party’s powerful conservative and evangelical wings. His Mormon faith makes evangelicals uneasy and his past record as a moderate Republican who supported abortion rights and introduced a prototype for Obama’s healthcare plan in Massachusetts makes him anathema to Tea Party activists. Romney is trying to reinvent himself as a ‘severe conservative’, but no-one really seems to be buying it.

Newt Gingrich: The Embodiment of Modern Republicanism?

So how do we explain this bizarre state of affairs? Why are Republican voters so reluctant to get behind a candidate who is almost certain to do better against President Obama than any of his rivals? One could be tempted to argue that this is simply an example of the Republican party lurching to the right and that primary voters are punishing Romney for not being sufficiently conservative. This would certainly fit the dominant media narrative about the Tea Party and the radicalisation of the Republican party. However, I am not convinced that ideology is the main reason why Republican voters are so reluctant to embrace Romney. After all, Newt Gingrich is hardly a paragon of conservative virtue. This is the man who sat on a sofa with Nancy Pelosi to warn about the dangers of climate change and who made millions of dollars from acting as a lobbyist for the government-backed mortgage company, Freddie Mac. If Republican voters were purely motivated by ideological concerns, then they would surely be flocking to the banners of Rick Santorum, a true social and fiscal conservative. But Santorum is still languishing in the single digits in most national polls.

Instead, I want to advance a different theory about the 2012 Republican primary race. My theory can be expressed in the form of a syllogism:

Let’s start with the premise that the Republican party, as it currently exists, is best understood as a coalition between two groups: cultural conservatives and economic conservatives.

The cultural conservatives are motivated by a fear of social decline. They look at issues like abortion, gay marriage, the breakdown of the traditional family, rising crime rates and the teaching of evolution in schools and they see a society that is slowly degenerating. The core of their political philosophy is a desire to arrest this social decline and to restore traditional social values. They are commonly referred to as the ‘religious right’ and are mostly drawn from the evangelical Christian community.

The economic conservatives are motivated by a fear of economic decline. They look at issues like the national debt, the size of government, levels of taxation and government regulation and they see a country that is on the brink of economic collapse. The core of their political philosophy is a desire to reverse this economic decline by shrinking the size of government and unleashing the power of the free market. They are commonly referred to as the ‘pro-business’ or ‘small government’ wing of the Republican party and are mostly drawn from the business community and the affluent middle-classes.

In the past, these two groups have been held together by a common enemy. In the 1980s it was the Soviet Union and the threat of international communism. After 9/11 it was Islamic fundamentalism and the threat of international terrorism. As long as America was facing a powerful external threat, the two wings of the Republican party could unite in the name of national security and patriotism. But now the Soviet Union is gone and Osama Bin Laden is dead. The glue that held the Republican coalition together has begun to dissolve. This is not to say that the two groups have nothing in common. Both believe passionately in the idea of American exceptionalism and both want to see America retain its status as the world’s sole superpower. But the lack of a common enemy has led to a change in emphasis. Without an external threat to focus on, both groups have increasingly turned their attention to domestic affairs. Cultural conservatives have become more concerned with fighting the culture war at home, whilst economic conservatives have become more concerned with reducing the size of government.

This brings me to the 2012 Republican primary race. The reason why Republican voters are so dissatisfied with their choice of candidates is that none of the candidates on offer is capable of appealing to both wings of the party. On the one hand we have Mitt Romney, the quintessential economic conservative. Romney’s whole campaign is based around the idea that he is a successful businessman who knows how to create jobs and fix the economy. But his past record as a social moderate means that he has no credibility with cultural conservatives. He can talk the talk on social issues, but no-one really believes that his heart is in it. On the other hand we have Rick Santorum, the quintessential cultural conservative. Santorum is a devout Catholic who has made his name as a champion of traditional family values. But he has little to say about the economy and his past record of supporting big government programmes means that he has no credibility with economic conservatives. As for the other candidates, they are all flawed in one way or another. Newt Gingrich tries to appeal to both wings of the party, but his personal history makes him unacceptable to many cultural conservatives, whilst his record as a Washington insider makes him unacceptable to many economic conservatives. Rick Perry should have been the perfect candidate on paper, a pro-business, evangelical Christian from a Southern state. But his poor debating skills and his past support for giving state benefits to illegal immigrants have destroyed his credibility.

So what does this all mean for the future of the Republican party? Well, in the short-term it probably means that Mitt Romney will win the nomination. He has the money, the organisation and the backing of the party establishment. But he will emerge from the primary process as a badly damaged candidate who will struggle to enthuse the party’s conservative base. He will then go on to lose the general election to Barack Obama, probably by a significant margin. In the long-term, it probably means that the Republican party is heading for a period of internal conflict and realignment. The uneasy coalition between cultural and economic conservatives is breaking down. The party is going to have to decide whether its future lies with the evangelical Christians of the heartland or with the secular, pro-business voters of the suburbs. It cannot be the party of both Rick Santorum and Mitt Romney. It has to choose.

Of course, I could be wrong about all of this. The Republican party has a powerful survival instinct and it may well be that the prospect of another four years of Barack Obama will be enough to unite the party’s warring factions. But, for what it’s worth, that’s my theory. And I am hoping I am wrong.

title: A theme in responses to critics found in the…
author: Jay Rosen
excerpt: A common theme in responses to critics is that the critic "just doesn't get it." This is a valid point, but it can also be a way of dismissing criticism without engaging with it. Rosen examines this tactic, particularly in political and online discussions, and explores why it's used and what it means.
summary: A recurring pattern in responses to criticism involves claiming the critic "just doesn't get it," often employed to avoid directly addressing the substance of the critique. This tactic is frequently used by politicians, pundits, and online commentators. Rosen identifies two potential causes: a simple misunderstanding stemming from differing ideas of clarity, or deliberate vagueness in the initial statement. The latter allows speakers to maintain flexibility, deflecting criticism by claiming misinterpretation or difficulty on the critic's part, enabling them to present ideas without the risk of being clearly contradicted. Rosen observes this trend particularly in online discussions about social media, blogging, and politics, prompting an examination of its frequent use.

key_concepts: The Production of Innocence, Church of the Savvy

pull_quote: This way of responding to critics seems to immunize Christianity against any rational criticism. For any objection, no matter how powerful, one can always draw a distinction that the critic has failed to draw.
raw_text:
I’ve been reading some Christian apologetics literature lately, and I’ve noticed a curious theme in the responses to critics. The apologist will take on an objection to Christianity from a critic, and then show that the objection is misguided, because the critic failed to notice some subtle but important distinction that Christianity makes. Let me show you what I mean. I’ll give some examples from a recent issue of the Christian Research Journal.

In a recent issue of the Christian Research Journal (Vol. 33/No. 05/2010), there is an article entitled, “Making Biblical Scholarship More Biblical,” by Craig Blomberg. In the article, Blomberg responds to several critics of Christian scholarship. Here is a typical exchange.

The critics charge that the Christian scholars are biased, and that this fatally compromises their scholarship.

Blomberg replies that the charge of bias is misguided. He distinguishes between two kinds of bias, the bad kind and the good kind. Here is Blomberg:

> On the other hand, if by bias one simply means a predisposition or a certain perspective, then no one is without bias. To suggest that only conservative Christians are biased is amazingly naive. Everyone comes to every issue with a certain worldview, a set of philosophical presuppositions, or a grid of beliefs that have been shaped by one’s upbringing, education, and experiences. To have a bias in this sense is not necessarily a bad thing. If one has good reasons for one’s predispositions, they may well be accurate. If one’s worldview corresponds to reality, it will be an asset, not a liability, to one’s scholarship. So the issue is not whether one has a bias but whether one has the correct bias. (p. 8)

So the critic has misfired. The critic has confused good bias with bad bias. Christian scholars have the good kind of bias, because their bias corresponds to reality. Thus, the charge is refuted.

In the same issue of the Journal, there is an article by Francis J. Beckwith, “Substance, Souls and Human Beings.” In it, he is responding to the charge by critics that the Christian view of the human person as an immaterial soul is incoherent. The critics point out that we often seem to refer to human persons in purely physical ways that don’t make sense on the view that a human person is an immaterial soul. For example, when we say “I see John walking,” we seem to be talking about a physical body, John’s body.

Beckwith argues that the critics have failed to appreciate a subtle distinction. Here is Beckwith:

> Why did the author not write, “I see John’s animated body walking”? The answer is simple and does not count against the substantial nature of persons. It is because of the difference between the “is” of identity and the “is” of predication. When I say that the man walking on the sidewalk is my brother, the “is” communicates identity. My brother and the man walking on the sidewalk are one and the same being. But when I say that my brother is a man with a body, the “is” communicates predication. I am attributing a property to my brother (a man with a body) and not claiming that my brother and the property of having a body are identical. Similarly, when I say that I see John walking down the street, I am using “John” to refer to a substance that has a collection of properties, including a physical body, that is undergoing a certain change (walking down the street). I am not claiming that the person John is identical to his body. (p. 16)

So the critic has misfired. The critic failed to notice the subtle distinction between the “is” of identity and the “is” of predication. Once that distinction is in view, the objection is seen to have no force.

Finally, in the same issue, there is an article by Paul Copan and Charles Taliaferro, “Is the God of the Old Testament a Moral Monster?” The authors take up the charge by critics that the Christian God, as portrayed in the Old Testament, is a moral monster. The critics point to the fact that God commanded the Israelites to kill all the men, women and children in Canaan. Copan and Taliaferro argue that the critics have misfired. They have failed to notice a subtle point of biblical interpretation.

> So what about the harsh-sounding language in Deuteronomy? We should point out that the deliberate rhetoric of warfare in the ancient Near East (ANE) was not meant to be taken literally. The language is strong, full of hyperbole, and stereotyped. We see this in Deuteronomy, Joshua, and other ANE texts. God, who accommodates himself to the ANE cultural setting, uses this conventional, exaggerated rhetoric of warfare to stress the importance of Israel’s taking possession of the land.

So the command in Deuteronomy to kill all the men, women and children was not meant to be taken literally. It was just an exaggeration.

It would be interesting to go through the contemporary apologetics literature to see how many responses to critics rely on this device. When a critic claims that Christianity is unreasonable, the apologist responds by drawing a distinction the critic has failed to draw. Once the distinction is made, the objection evaporates. The critic is shown to be unsubtle and obtuse.

This way of responding to critics seems to immunize Christianity against any rational criticism. For any objection, no matter how powerful, one can always draw a distinction that the critic has failed to draw. Consider the problem of evil. The critic argues that an all-good, all-powerful God would not permit the suffering we see in the world. The apologist replies that the critic has failed to distinguish between gratuitous suffering and non-gratuitous suffering. God permits only non-gratuitous suffering. So the critic has misfired.

This theme is so prevalent in the Christian apologetics literature, and in so many different contexts, that one begins to wonder whether it reveals a mindset. A mindset that finds a way to deflect any and all criticism, and that always finds a way to show that Christianity is reasonable after all. One wonders what, if anything, would count as disconfirming evidence for theism?

title: Three different kinds of context were missing
author: Jay Rosen
excerpt: This comment discusses three different kinds of context missing from exchanges about Hayek's work, focusing on the problem being addressed, the intellectual tradition Hayek was working within, and the arguments within his essay "Economics and Knowledge." The central problem for Hayek was how a society of free individuals could produce an optimal allocation of resources given the division of knowledge.
summary: Rosen identifies three crucial kinds of context often missing in discussions of intellectual history, using Hayek's work as a case study. The first is the specific problem Hayek was addressing, which was how a society of free individuals could achieve optimal resource allocation despite dispersed knowledge. Second, the relevant intellectual tradition, namely the Austrian school, and Hayek's engagement with Mises and subjectivism, is essential. Lastly, the context of the arguments within Hayek's essay "Economics and Knowledge" itself clarifies his focus on coordinating decentralized knowledge through the market process rather than individual plan optimization. Rosen emphasizes that these contextual elements shape the interpretation of Hayek's ideas, differentiating them from the concerns of others like Robbins.

key_concepts: False balance

pull_quote: When you’re an expert in a field, you forget what it was like to be a novice. You forget that the things that seem obvious to you are not at all obvious to someone who’s just starting out. And so you fail to explain the context of your requests.
raw_text:
A decade ago Clay Shirky wrote what has turned out to be a foundational essay for my thinking about the web and the world, a piece called “A Group Is Its Own Worst Enemy.” The essay is about the challenges of fostering group conversation online, but the lessons are generalizable. The core of his argument is that social software needs to do more than just provide a platform for conversation. It needs to provide tools that help the group navigate the social dilemmas that inevitably arise as a group grows. The essay is filled with great lines, but for a long time this was my favorite:

> In the best of cases, the tensions that groups are trying to manage are not breakdowns in the system, but are in fact the system working as designed. A group trying to have a serious discussion is threatened by the arrival of a dozen newbies who want to talk about something else. The new users are not behaving badly, they are behaving normally. It is the job of the software to help the group negotiate that kind of conflict, rather than simply letting the majority overwhelm the minority, or letting the most committed group members scorch the earth around them to keep the discussion ‘pure’.

These two passages — one from a student, the other from a faculty member — are from a report published by the Ethnography of the University Initiative at the University of Illinois. I encountered them in a really terrific IHE piece by Scott Jaschik summarizing the report’s findings on the crucial and neglected role of context in student writing.

I want to use these passages, and the larger issues they raise, to think through three different kinds of context that are missing when we talk about technology and education. We’re not very good at putting our tools in context. More specifically, we’re not very good at putting our tools in these three contexts in particular. And I want to suggest that this is a particularly acute problem in higher education, where our tools are often themselves decontextualized.

The Context of Alternatives

I’m really struck by the way the student in the first passage frames her complaint about her professor. She doesn’t seem to be complaining about the requirement that she write a particular kind of essay. She’s complaining about the professor’s failure to explain what makes the required essay different from the other kinds of essays she’s used to writing. As the authors of the report put it, “Students felt that faculty assumed students knew what faculty wanted, when in fact students felt they lacked the context for a particular assignment.”

This is a classic problem of expertise. When you’re an expert in a field, you forget what it was like to be a novice. You forget that the things that seem obvious to you are not at all obvious to someone who’s just starting out. And so you fail to explain the context of your requests. You fail to explain the alternatives.

When we talk about technology in education, we often make the same mistake. We talk about the virtues of a particular tool without explaining what makes it better than the alternatives. We talk about the power of social media without explaining how it’s different from the other kinds of media that students are used to. We talk about the importance of digital literacy without explaining how it’s different from the other kinds of literacy that students have been taught.

The Context of History

The faculty member in the second passage is also complaining about a lack of context, but of a different kind. She’s complaining about the fact that her students don’t seem to understand the history of the discipline they’re studying. They don’t understand that the way we do things now is not the way we’ve always done them. They don’t understand that the questions we’re asking now are not the questions we’ve always asked.

This is a problem of historical consciousness. It’s the inability to see the present as a product of the past. It’s the inability to see that the way we do things now is not the only way they could be done.

When we talk about technology in education, we often make the same mistake. We talk about the latest and greatest tools without any sense of how they fit into the larger history of educational technology. We talk about the promise of online learning without any sense of the long and complicated history of distance education. We talk about the power of the iPad without any sense of the long and complicated history of the book.

The Context of Implementation

But even if we do a good job of explaining the context of alternatives and the context of history, we still have to deal with the context of implementation. We still have to figure out how to actually use the tools we’ve chosen. We still have to figure out how to make them work in our particular classrooms, with our particular students.

And this is where things get really tricky. Because the context of implementation is always local. It’s always specific. It’s always contingent. What works in one classroom might not work in another. What works with one group of students might not work with another.

This is why the faculty member in the second passage is so frustrated. She’s not just frustrated that her students don’t know the history of the discipline. She’s frustrated that they don’t know how to do the work of the discipline. They don’t know how to read and write and think like historians or literary critics or sociologists. They don’t know how to do the things that she knows how to do.

When we talk about technology in education, we often make the same mistake. We talk about the power of a particular tool without any sense of the practical challenges of using it. We talk about the virtues of a particular pedagogy without any sense of the hard work it takes to make it work. We talk about the promise of a particular reform without any sense of the political and institutional obstacles that stand in its way.

I was reminded of all of this when I read a recent post by Dan Meyer, in which he reflects on the difference between the way he used to teach and the way he teaches now. Dan is a math teacher, and he’s become something of a celebrity in the world of math education for his innovative use of technology. But what’s most striking about his post is not the technology he uses. It’s the way he thinks about his students. He’s obsessed with the question of what his students are thinking. He’s obsessed with the question of how they’re making sense of the world. He’s obsessed with the question of what they need to know in order to learn.

In other words, he’s obsessed with context. He’s obsessed with the context of alternatives, the context of history, and the context of implementation. And that’s why he’s such a good teacher. That’s why he’s so good at using technology to help his students learn. That’s why he asks the right questions.

raw_text:
Serious Journalism in the Age of Digital Networks
By Philip N. Howard on November 22, 2011

The following is an excerpt from my chapter in The Next Digital Decade: Essays on the Future of the Internet, edited by Berin Szoka and Adam Marcus.

Professional journalists are in the business of telling stories. So are citizen journalists, though they tend to have fewer constraints on their creativity and fewer professional norms to follow. Both kinds of journalists now ply their trade over a variety of information infrastructures—print, broadcast, and digital networks—and are more interconnected than ever before. There have been many predictions that the Internet will be the death of traditional journalism, but it seems more likely that the Internet is just beginning to save journalism from itself. The crisis in serious news reporting has more to do with the business of journalism than with digital networks. These networks, in fact, may force journalism to return to its roots in investigation and analysis.

For a long time, professional news media had an almost exclusive role in mediating between sources of information and the public. Most information had to pass through a journalist to become news. Over the last decade, however, many important sources of news now regularly break stories about themselves. Government agencies, corporations, political candidates, and celebrities all use digital networks to communicate directly with their publics. Twitter is now the source of many breaking news stories, but often the tweets come from primary sources or eyewitnesses, not journalists. Indeed, the people with real expertise—academics, civil servants, policy analysts—are often better at analyzing the news than professional journalists are. Bloggers are more transparent than professional journalists about their political biases, which is one reason why blogs are so popular. Social media provide ways for citizens to share the news they think is most important with their friends. Digital networks have not only disrupted the business model for traditional news organizations but also challenged their cultural authority as the sole source of high-quality news and analysis.

How can traditional news organizations compete? Probably by becoming much more like digital networks. They can do a better job of creating value with the content generated by digital networks. Instead of simply reporting the news, they can do a better job of explaining it.

There are many ways that information and communication technologies will help journalists do better investigative reporting and analysis. For example, by studying the structure of digital networks, we have new ways of knowing what news is. What kinds of people share what kinds of content with whom, and what does this say about the news? What kinds of stories capture the public’s imagination, and what do these patterns of attention tell us about the story? By studying the flow of ideas over social media, we can find out what parts of a story resonate with the public and what information citizens are using to make political and economic decisions. By studying the context of ideas in digital networks, we can learn what frames of analysis people bring to bear on a story, and what other ideas are closely associated with a story in the public’s mind.

The best data-visualizations about politics, culture, and society are not being done by news organizations. They are being produced by computer scientists, graphic artists, and social scientists who have an interest in information visualization. Data-visualizations can tell very interesting and important stories about large data sets—often much better than a single journalist can. The best analyses of political trends are not being done by news organizations, but by bloggers like Nate Silver at fivethirtyeight.com. He does a better job of analyzing political polls than anyone else in the business because he knows what he is talking about, is transparent about his methods and his data, and engages his readers in a constant conversation about his work. He uses the network to improve his product.

Professional journalists have a critical role to play in producing serious news, but this is a role they must now share. Their comparative advantage is no longer in telling us what is happening, because we can learn this from multiple other sources. Rather, their real value-added will be in investigating and explaining why something is happening. The news organizations that do original research and employ multiple analytical perspectives will be the ones that succeed. Professional journalists can learn from social networks, and learn to be network analysts.

Digital networks provide powerful new opportunities for investigative reporting. Most obviously, journalists can do a better job of using search engines and databases to get information. Search can be used to generate lists of sources, find experts, and generate context for stories. Databases can be used to reveal patterns of political and economic activity. Such investigative work is often called “computer-assisted reporting,” but this phrase reveals a bias in how journalists think about technology. When we use the telephone to interview a source, we do not call it “telephone-assisted reporting.” Digital tools are now just as indispensable as the telephone for good journalism. In fact, journalists need to build their own tools for parsing digital information, and many journalism schools now offer courses that teach programming skills.

But digital networks do more than simply provide new tools for individual journalists; they are also a new source of content and a new platform for disseminating investigative work. The public is often the source of valuable tips and insights for investigative work, but in the age of digital networks this resource can be put to work on a much larger scale. When news organizations are willing to share their raw data—the interview notes, documents, and data sets that are the basis of an investigation—they are often rewarded with additional content and analysis from an engaged public. For example, The Guardian opened up its data on the expense accounts of Members of Parliament (MPs) and invited readers to help review the documents. The project revealed the scope of this political scandal much faster than the newspaper’s journalists could have acting on their own. The newspaper created a simple web application that allowed readers to search the data, tag items of interest, and share what they found. Similarly, ProPublica has begun posting large data sets online so that other journalists and the public can work with their data. ProPublica journalist Amanda Michel has argued that news organizations need to do more than just build editorial teams—they need to build communities around their reporting.

If news organizations make their data public, is this investigative journalism or something else? I think so. In an age of information abundance, investigative work takes on a special significance. What stories are worth investigating? What are the special analytical and visualization tools that news organizations can bring to bear? Most importantly, how will a news organization get its investigative work to the largest possible audience?

A small but growing number of journalists are learning how to build their own databases from public records, structure queries to generate stories, and generate compelling visualizations. A small but growing number of news organizations are learning how to build editorial teams that include computer scientists, graphic artists, and social scientists. Such teams can work together to manage large data sets, generate multiple stories, and present investigative reporting in compelling ways for different audiences through different media. Today’s journalists need to be more than good storytellers; they need to be good managers of complex information.

In The Next Digital Decade, we will see several important trends in journalism mature. First, we will see more news organizations forming partnerships with university researchers, technology firms, and other media outlets to do investigative reporting. Good investigative reporting is expensive and time-consuming, but the costs can be spread among organizations that have different skill sets. Second, we will see more news organizations developing editorial teams with diverse forms of expertise. Computer programmers, social scientists, and graphic artists will work with journalists to develop multiple stories from complex data for multiple audiences. Third, we will see more investigative work that explicitly models the structure of social life and the flow of information. Social network analysis provides a powerful set of tools for investigating social relations and tracing the flow of ideas and influence among actors in a network. Finally, we will see more investigative work that is presented in dynamic ways. Web-based visualizations of complex data will become the norm. The data behind such visualizations will be made available to the public for further exploration.

Investigative journalism has always been a conversation between sources, reporters, and the public. With digital media, this conversation takes on a new form. Digital networks are not just a new medium for news; they provide a new way of conceptualizing what news is. News has always been a social construction, the product of editors and journalists making choices about what to cover. Today, the public plays a much more important role in constructing the news. Social media provide a way of collecting, sharing, and ranking stories. A story’s importance is now determined not only by editors but also by the number of people who read, comment on, and share it with their friends.

The future of serious journalism lies in its past. Digital networks provide powerful new ways for journalists to do what they have always done best: investigate stories and provide analysis. The technologies of the next digital decade will give journalists new tools for researching stories, new platforms for presenting their findings, and new ways of engaging the public in a conversation about the news. The stories that journalists tell will increasingly be about networks of people, organizations, and ideas. The serious news organizations that best understand these new networks of exchange, and best connect their investigative reporting to these flows of information, will thrive in the next digital decade.

raw_text:
Arming us not with knowledge of, but acquaintance with
September 16, 2010

This is a great quote from Walter Benjamin on how the deluge of information doesn’t necessarily make us smarter:

For the ancients, the ‘memorizable’ was the highest form of knowledge, because it was assimilated into their very being, while for us the highest form is that which can be ‘looked up’ – that is, that which isalienated from us but which we can retrieve at will. The world has ceased to be a fabric of correspondences and has become a space of objects.

There is some truth to this, especially for those of us who came of age with the Internet. It has radically changed our relationship to information and, by extension, knowledge.

Memory has ceased to be something internal and personal, and has become a machine that lives outside of us. There’s a wonderful passage in Plato’s Phaedrus that expresses the ancient world’s anxiety about the arrival of writing as a technology. In a dialogue between the god Theuth and the king Thamus, the latter argues against the technology of writing, saying that it is not a recipe for memory, but for reminding. It will create forgetfulness in the learners’ souls, because they will not use their memories; they will trust to the external written characters and not remember of themselves.

Now, as one observer of information overload put it, we are armed not with knowledge of things, but acquaintance with them.

This is not to say that education has become less rigorous or demanding. In many ways, the opposite is true. We are now expected to be able to find and synthesize information on an unprecedented scale. The key skill is no longer memorization, but the ability to search, filter, and organize.

Of course, there is a certain danger to this way of learning. We can become so focused on the process of finding information that we lose sight of the bigger picture. We can become so accustomed to the instant gratification of a Google search that we lose the patience for deeper, more reflective forms of thought.

raw_text:
This is not my post, it is a Jay Rosen’s one. But it is such a good one that I am reproducing it here for my own reference and to spread the word.

The people formerly known as the audience are those who were on the receiving end of a media system that ran one way, in a broadcasting pattern, with high entry fees and a few firms competing to speak loudly while the rest of the population listened in isolation from one another— and who today are not in a situation like that at all.

Think of passengers on a ship who have just discovered that they are all sailors. People who were once media consumers are now producers of it too, and they are not only producers but participants in a massive conversation. We know that. It’s what Web 2.0 means. But the implications are still sinking in for we who were once the media.

Our relationship to the people formerly known as the audience has to change. If they are no longer just the audience but participants in a conversation, then we cannot just broadcast to them. We have to join the conversation with them. The days when our voice was the only one that mattered are over. That’s why I say that the watchword for the press is not objectivity, but transparency. What does that mean? It means journalists have to show their work and reveal, to the degree they can, how they came to their conclusions.

The people formerly known as the audience are starting to get good at this. Just look at what they do on Wikipedia. And journalists can do it too. They can explain who they are, where they’re coming from, what they’re trying to do, what they think their mission is. All of that is part of transparency. They can ask the people formerly known as the audience for help. And they can point to the better work of the people formerly known as the audience, and link to it, and be a part of it. The conversation is not a lecture. It’s a conversation. To be a part of it, journalists have to listen to the people formerly known as the audience. This used to be called letters to the editor. Now it’s called a community online. But the community is smarter than the letters column, because the community is talking to each other, not just to us.

We have to be a part of that conversation because it is the new news system. This used to happen at the coffee shop, or at the office. But now it is a permanent part of the online world. So journalists have to know what the conversation is and be a part of it to do their jobs well. And that is the change.

Read the whole text at Jay Rosen’s blog, Press Think

Get there by clicking a link and the New York Times paywall disappears
In Wednesday’s big announcement about the New York Times’ plans to start charging for online content, there was one detail that pretty much negates the entire paywall plan:

Readers who come to NYTimes.com through links from search engines like Google and social networks like Facebook and Twitter will be able to read those articles for free, even if they have reached their monthly reading limit.

That’s right: as long as you click a link from another site, the paywall disappears. Even if you want to read an article on the front page of the New York Times’ Web site, you won’t have to pay. All you have to do is copy the article’s headline, paste it into Google’s search bar and then click on the link to the story. Voila! Free access.

If it’s a smart paywall the Times is looking for, then this is not it. It doesn’t even make a distinction between heavy and light users: as long as you know the Google trick, you can read as much as you want.

For me, the main reason I go directly to a news organization’s Web site is to browse. I want to see what the day’s top stories are and how they’re being played. For that reason, I go to nytimes.com, washingtonpost.com, wsj.com and latimes.com almost every day. It seems to me that the Times’ paywall plan gives me an incentive not to go directly to their site. It encourages me to use other sites, like Google News and the Huffington Post, to browse the Times’ content.

Still, the New York Times’ paywall plan is smarter than the one implemented by Newsday last year. That newspaper’s Web site is a ghost town now.

Of course, this raises one other question: just how easy is it going to be to find a link to a New York Times story? Perhaps they’ll change their terms of service, making it so that only certain sites can link to their content. Maybe they’ll even disable linking altogether, committing Web site suicide. I doubt it, but who knows?

raw_text:
My Simple Fix for the Messed-Up Sunday Shows

Everyone knows the Sunday morning political talk shows are broken. The format, the guests, the moderators, the questions, the answers, the punditry — they are all, for the most part, a complete waste of time. Endless bloviating, constant interruptions, pointless questions, filibustering talking points, rampant spinning, unchallenged lies, and a general lack of substance dominate the airwaves.

But the Sunday shows are still a big deal in Washington. Being booked is a sign of importance. Performing well is a sign of influence. So, every Sunday, millions of Americans tune in and get nothing but an earful of hot air.

There have been many proposals floated on how to fix the shows, from banning politicians to banning talking points. But most of those would be difficult to implement. My solution is simple, easy to implement and would bring a level of accountability — and entertainment — to the programs.

My solution is a simple shot clock. Think of it as a chess clock for talking heads.

Here is how it would work:

1. A time limit for answers. After a moderator asks a question, the guest has a fixed amount of time to answer. Let’s say 60 seconds. At the end of that time, a buzzer goes off and their microphone is cut. No more endless talking points. No more filibustering. Just answer the damn question. If they have more to say, too bad. They had their chance. Sixty seconds is plenty of time to give a thoughtful and complete answer. And if a guest consistently fails to answer the question, the moderator can just stop asking them questions.

2. A time limit for follow-ups. Often a moderator will ask a follow-up to a guest’s answer. When they do, another time limit goes into effect. Let’s say 30 seconds. A simple follow-up doesn’t require another long-winded response. It requires a straight answer. So, 30 seconds should be plenty of time to get it. And if they can’t do it in 30 seconds, the buzzer will do it for them.

3. The “put up or shut up” rule. There is nothing worse than when one guest attacks another guest or a third-party and that other person is not there to defend himself. So, from now on, that is forbidden. If you want to say something bad about someone, that person has to be in the studio with you so they can respond. And when that happens, my shot clock is suspended. A little unmoderated back-and-forth can be a good thing. Let them have at it.

4. A penalty box. If a guest repeatedly violates the rules, they get sent to a penalty box. Their microphone is cut, their chair is moved to the corner of the studio and they have to sit there quietly until the segment is over. Public humiliation is a great motivator.

5. A truth-o-meter. We now have the ability to do instantaneous fact-checking. So let’s put it to use. Each show should have a team of fact-checkers. And when a guest tells a lie or misrepresents the truth, a giant “bullshit” graphic should flash on the screen. Maybe a buzzer should go off, too. Nothing stops a liar in his tracks more than being called out on his lies in real-time.

I guarantee these new rules would make for better television. The shows would be more informative and more entertaining. And guests would have a real incentive to be more honest and more direct. We might actually learn something.

The Sunday morning talk shows can be fixed. All it takes is a little creativity and a backbone. And if not, there is always ESPN Classic.

title: Eight Key Terms For Determining Legitimacy In Journalism
author: Jay Rosen
excerpt: Eight key terms for determining legitimacy in journalism include expertise, independence, objectivity, transparency, accountability, impartiality, public interest, and verification. These terms are crucial for ensuring news is credible, trustworthy, and serves the public good.
summary: Legitimacy in journalism hinges on several key terms. Expertise is demonstrated through experience and knowledge. Independence, crucial for separating news from propaganda, requires journalists to avoid being swayed by external agendas. Objectivity involves presenting stories fairly and accurately. Transparency demands that journalists disclose their sources and methods. Accountability requires taking responsibility for errors and upholding ethical standards. Impartiality means treating all parties equally. Serving the public interest, by providing relevant information and promoting informed debate, is essential. Verification, through cross-referencing and fact-checking, is crucial for maintaining credibility, especially in the era of misinformation. These elements work together to ensure news is trustworthy and serves the public good.

raw_text:
These thoughts grew from a comment thread at Nieman Lab. The post in question was titled: The news Good Housekeeping seal: What makes a nonprofit outlet legit? Such things as: adherence to the Society of Professional Journalists code of ethics, submitting entries for professional prizes and holding a press credential from a federal or state body were said to be good proxies for legitimacy in journalism.  I objected to this:

I don’t think “professionalism” is a feature of legitimacy at all. We could say it’s one way of attempting to secure legitimacy, but the equation: professional news person = legitimate provider of news does not work. Nor does the reverse: you’re legit if you’re recognizably a professional.

Other than Jayson Blair, is there anyone associated with the New York Times who undermined its legitimacy more than Judith Miller? I can’t think of anyone. And yet after the revelations of what she did in the Plame case came out, the Society of Professional Journalists (SPJ) gave her a First Amendment award. Her lack of legitimacy spread to the society. Are you aware what percentage of SPJ members are in fact public relations people? If you find out, you might be more circumspect.

Submitting for prizes guarantees nothing. They do not belong on your list at all. Nor do credentials. Check out the way the professionals in charge of granting press credentials behave when it comes to getting new providers into the Senate press gallery in DC. If you look into it, you’ll discover thin to zero legitimacy, but a lot of behavior that is typical of professionals. Is the Washington Independent a legitimate news provider? I bet if you looked at it you’d say yes. Find out if they can get credentials.

In reply, the author of the Nieman Lab post, Jim Barnett, said, “Hey, help a fellow. What would you say are some easily discernable, objective criteria to gauge legitimacy? How would you get past the Potter Stewart test?” He was referring, of course, to Justice Stewart’s definition of hard core pornography, “I know it when I see it.”  So this is what I told him:

I know many people love that Potter Stewart quote but I don’t see much of a difference between, “I know it when I see it,” and “Actually, I haven’t a clue.” 

What would you say are some easily discernable, objective criteria to gauge legitimacy?

I’d start with the will to veracity, also known as truthtelling. Truthtelling even when it hurts or causes problems for your friends. Real journalists tell us what happened because it actually happened that way, and not some other way. All forms of legitimacy derive from this one.

Then I’d move on to a manifest concern for accuracy, as in getting it right and correcting it when wrong.

Third pillar: transparency, also called disclosure, so we know where you’re coming from and what your stake is in the matter under review, if any.

Intellectual honesty: like when you paraphrase what Senator Brown says it actually does capture what Senator Brown says. This is sometimes called “fairness,” but I think my term is more descriptive.

Currency, in the sense that you are trying to report what happened recently, to keep up with events and what is known now. Journalism is about the present, not what was true six months or six years ago. Legitimacy in journalism has something to do with a determination to keep us up to date with a shifting world.

Inquiry: not the perfect word but the closest fit I can find. I refer to the drive to find out, to inquire and reveal more than what lies on the surface. We all know of situations in which the person in question didn’t lie but also didn’t try… to find out. That’s what I mean by inquiry: trying to find out. Journalism, to be journalism, must do that.

Utility, sometimes called by another name: public service. Journalists can get into legitimacy problems when they are trying to find out, but finding out serves no public purpose. Their legitimacy is clearest when the public interest is served by what they are striving to reveal to us.

Veracity, accuracy, transparency, intellectual honesty, currency, inquiry, utility.  That’s where I would start in attempting to define legitimacy in journalism. Providers of news, information and commentary who devote themselves to those seven things are solid citizens of Legit-a-land.

I have to add one more, but you will probably hate me for it because it will strike you as jargon, and all journalists claim to hate jargon (but “lede” is okay, right?) Anyway, my eighth pillar of legitimacy is polyphonicity. I know: awful term! It means “more than one sound.”

Journalism to be fully legitimate needs to present a plurality of voices, not just one.  I don’t mean to invoke the gods of balance. They are false gods. I mean to suggest that journalism isn’t a monologue. More than one person speaks in it. More than one angle is taken on the object.

Now I am sure you noticed that among my eight key terms for determining legitimacy in journalism one does not find such things as: objectivity, professionalism, “code of ethics,” balance, getting paid, being incorporated as a commercial business, working full time at newsgathering, eschewing opinion, bearing a press pass, or getting certified by the (journalistic) powers that be.

These are shortcuts, and taking shortcuts is not… legitimate!

raw_text:
What I Told the Man from Politics Daily

Carl Lavin of Politics Daily called me Friday to get my reaction to this story: “White House Escalates War on Fox News.” The headline is from Politico. Lavin wanted to know: had there ever been anything like it? The White House trying to de-legitimize a news organization? I said I would have to think about that. But I had a reaction to his question. This is what I told him.

What you are witnessing is the de-bugging of the software that runs in the heads of Washington journalists. The software is called, “the view from nowhere.”

For a long time, the software had a bug in it. It was this: if you were a big enough media company, and you looked and sounded like a news organization, and you said you were a news organization, you were treated as one by the Washington press. That was the bug. The software directed journalists to apply their neutrality codes to you and grant you all the privileges of a “player” in the Washington game. And of course you got a seat in the White House press room.

Now the White House has announced that it will not treat Fox News as a news organization, but as a political opponent. And this is forcing journalists to confront the bug in their software. Because Fox is a big media company that looks and sounds like a news organization and says it’s a news organization. And it gets huge ratings. And for a lot of people in the U.S. it is the most trusted name in news.

So the software says: treat Fox as a news organization. But the White House says: we’re not going to. Fox is the voice of the opposition. We’re not going to treat them like they are a news organization.

And the software can’t handle that. It stalls. You get the blue screen of death. Or a weird error message comes up on the screen. It might say, “Is the White House trying to… de-legitimize a news organization?” Because that’s what the software can compute.

But if you debug the software you might find that the problem is not what the White House is doing, but what Fox News is doing. Which is: practicing a different kind of journalism. One that is not based on the view from nowhere.

And the software can’t handle that. So what do you get? You get a story about how the White House is escalating its war on Fox. And you get a lot of journalists talking about whether the White House should be trying to de-legitimize a news organization. You get Carl Lavin calling me.

I said to Lavin: I can’t tell you whether it’s a smart political move for the White House to do this. I don’t know. I can’t tell you if it will work. I don’t know. I can’t tell you if it’s an effective use of White House time and energy. I don’t know. But I can tell you what it means for journalism.

It means that the software is being de-bugged.

And I told him that I for one am glad to see it. It’s long overdue. For ten years I have been describing what Fox News does as a different kind of journalism. Not better, not worse, just different. It’s a post-modern form. In a way it’s more honest. Fox News has a point of view. It has a purpose. It is trying to accomplish something in the world of politics.

The view from nowhere also has a purpose, but it can’t say what it is. It has to pretend that it doesn’t have a purpose, that it is just there to tell you what happened. It has to pretend that it doesn’t have a point of view. It has to pretend that it is just a mirror on the world.

But it isn’t a mirror. It’s a lens. And the lens has a focus. And the focus is on the powerful. The view from nowhere is the view from Washington. It is the view of the people who run the country. It is the view of the insiders. And it is the view that they want everyone else to have.

So when the White House says, “we’re not going to treat Fox as a news organization,” they are not attacking the press. They are attacking the view from nowhere. They are saying, “we are not going to pretend that you are just a mirror. We are going to treat you as a player. We are going to treat you as an opponent.”

And the software can’t handle that. The software crashes.

And this is what I told the man from Politics Daily. He quoted me fairly and accurately in his story. But he didn’t use my best line. So I am using it here.

What I mean is that there are two different kinds of journalism in America today. One is based on the view from nowhere. The other is not. And the two are at war. And the war is not between the left and the right. It is between the view from nowhere and the view from somewhere.

And the White House has just decided which side it is on.

So the question is not whether the White House is trying to de-legitimize a news organization. The question is: what is a news organization? And that’s a question that the software can’t answer.

I got that line from Clay Shirky. He said it in a different context, but it applies here. What is a news organization? Is it a big building with a lot of reporters and editors and a printing press? Is it a website with a lot of traffic? Is it a TV channel with a lot of viewers?

Or is it a group of people who are trying to find out what is going on and tell other people about it?

If it’s the latter, then Fox News is a news organization. And so is the New York Times. And so is Talking Points Memo. And so is the Huffington Post. And so is this blog.

But they are all practicing different kinds of journalism. And the difference is not in their methods. It is in their purposes.

The New York Times is trying to tell you what happened yesterday. Talking Points Memo is trying to get to the bottom of a story. The Huffington Post is trying to change the world. And Fox News is trying to win elections.

These are all legitimate purposes. But they are not the same purpose. And they produce different kinds of journalism. And the software can’t handle that. The software wants to treat them all the same. It wants to apply the same rules to all of them. It wants to pretend that they are all just trying to tell you what happened.

But they’re not. And the White House knows they’re not. And that is why the White House is doing what it is doing. It is trying to de-bug the software.

It’s about time.

Update: Carl Lavin’s story is up: White House vs. Fox News: A New Escalation. It quotes me this way:

“What you are witnessing is the de-bugging of the software that runs in the heads of Washington journalists,” said Jay Rosen, who teaches journalism at New York University and writes the PressThink blog. The software, he said, tells journalists that “if you were a big enough media company and you looked and sounded like a news organization, and you said you were a news organization, you were treated as one by the Washington press.”

That’s fine. I just think my line about the blue screen of death was better.

Another update: A reader emails to say I am naive to think the White House is doing this for the reasons I say. “They are doing it because it works for them politically. It fires up their base. It makes them look tough. It’s a smart move. And you are falling for it.”

I agree that it’s a smart move. But I don’t think I’m falling for it. I am trying to understand what it means for journalism. And I think it means that the software is being de-bugged.

Whether the White House knows that it is de-bugging the software is another question. I doubt that they do. But that doesn’t matter. What matters is that it’s happening. And it’s a good thing.

Final update: Here’s a thought for journalists who are covering this story. Instead of asking “is the White House trying to de-legitimize a news organization,” why not ask “is Fox News a news organization?”

That’s a much more interesting question. And it’s one that the software can’t answer.

I myself think the press is slowly but surely fracturing into two. There is the press that maintains the view from nowhere, which is the institutional press centered in Washington. And there is the press that has a point of view, which is the rest of us. They can both be called news organizations, and they both practice journalism. But they are not the same thing. Increasingly, when I speak of the press I have to specify which one I mean. When Lavin of Politics Daily called me, I knew he meant the Washington press because of where he works. But the question is becoming: what does that phrase even mean?

raw_text:
How to know if you are behaving ethically as a journalist: Jay Rosen’s checklist

Jay Rosen, journalism professor at New York University, has a useful 10-point checklist to help reporters work out whether they are treating the people they are reporting on fairly and ethically.

1. If you were on the receiving end of the story you are reporting and writing, would you feel that you were being treated fairly?

2. If your report were a mirror, would the people you are reporting on recognize themselves in it?

3. Before you publish the story, have you done all you can to get the response of the people you are reporting on, especially people who will be portrayed in a negative light?

4. Are you confident that you have given the people in your story a fair hearing?

5. If you were to look the people you are reporting on in the eye after your story was published, could you honestly say you’d done your best to be fair to them?

6. Are you willing to listen to the people you are reporting on, even after the story has been published?

7. Do you have a way for people to contact you?

8. Do you have a way of correcting your story if it is wrong?

9. Are you willing to consider that your story might be wrong, or unfair?

10. Are you ready to apologize if your story is wrong, or unfair?

You can read his original post here.

raw_text:
Jay Rosen’s “church of the savvy” explains a lot about the political press, but perhaps nowhere are its teachings applied more than in the coverage of Barack Obama.

Rosen defines it thusly:

Savviness is that quality of being “in the know,” wise to the ways of Washington, hip to the real players and how they move. The savvy don’t just report what is said; they tell us what it means. And what it means is that everything is political. Everything is about an election. Everything is tactical. There’s a rich vocabulary to support this. If a politician says something, he is “positioning” himself. If he shifts his position he is “reaching out” to a key “demographic.” His speech is “aimed” at a particular “constituency.” Everything is a move. The savvy press is not dumb. It knows that some moves are brilliant, some are boneheaded and some are just what you have to do to get re-elected. Which is of course the ultimate prize, the only one that matters.

It’s this church that insists that Obama’s call for a new brand of politics was merely a campaign slogan — a tactic, if you will — designed to appeal to the mushy middle, those who pine for a post-partisanship that will never happen because, well, it can’t. Because politics is what it is, and what it is is a cynical game. This is the first, and only, commandment of the savvy.

So when Obama made some very specific promises about transparency during the campaign, the church of the savvy was ready with an explanation: this was just a way to differentiate himself from the famously secretive Bush Administration. That’s what candidates do, after all. They promise change. That it doesn’t come is to be expected.

Which bring us to a story from last Friday’s Washington Post:

Obama, who campaigned on a pledge to make his administration the most transparent in U.S. history, has thus far failed to deliver on major promises to reform the way Washington does business and has in some cases taken steps to restrict the flow of information to the public, according to a review of his record by open-government advocates.

Most of the promises that Obama has broken have to do with the issue that government watchdogs consider paramount: shedding more light on the decision-making process in Washington. Despite a pledge to post all non-emergency bills on the White House Web site for five days before signing them, for example, the president has violated his policy on at least a half-dozen occasions. He has also preserved the Bush administration’s practice of maintaining the secrecy of White House visitor logs, and his administration has sided with its predecessor in a Supreme Court case involving the state secrets privilege.

To the church of the savvy, this is not news. Of course Obama said he’d post bills online for five days before signing them — it sounded good. A great line for a stump speech, but impractical in the real world. Of course he sided with the Bush administration on the state secrets privilege — that’s what presidents do. They amass power, they don’t give it away. Of course he failed to deliver on his pledge to make his administration the most transparent in U.S. history — that’s what politicians do. They promise change and then, once in office, become masters of the status quo. It would be naive to expect otherwise. It would not be savvy.

It’s this thinking that has led Politifact — usually a reliable source — to keep some of Obama’s transparency promises in the “in the works” or “stalled” categories on their “Obameter,” as if Obama’s failure to live up to them is a result of some process being held up. Perhaps a committee is studying the issue. In fact, these promises could be fulfilled with a single presidential directive. They aren’t because he doesn’t want them to be. Period.

It’s this same thinking that leads Jonathan Martin to write this:

It’s impossible to take at face value any president or presidential candidate vowing to change the ways of Washington.

It’s not just that they all do it, it’s that it’s such a fundamental part of running for the White House and, once there, wielding power.

Of course they do it. The question is whether we should accept it. The church of the savvy insists we should. It’s what being a grown-up is all about. Only children still believe in Santa Claus and campaign promises.

But if the press doesn’t believe that candidates mean what they say, what is the point of a campaign? Is it all just a show, a long-running political theater whose lines we all know by heart? Why not just skip the whole thing and flip a coin?

I suspect the press embraces savviness because it makes them feel like insiders. The rest of us may believe a candidate when he says he will do something, but they know better. They’ve seen it all before.

Here’s the thing: Obama’s calls for transparency may or may not have been sincere. As a candidate, I had no way of knowing what was in his heart. So I looked at what he said he would do. These were not vague promises of a new dawn. He said he would end the abuse of signing statements. He said he would close the revolving door that lets government officials cash in on their service. He said he would create a public database of all federal grants and contracts. He said he would not sign any non-emergency bill without posting it on the White House website for five days.

Either he meant it or he didn’t. Either he would do it or he wouldn’t. There was no third way.

I took him at his word, and hoped for the best.

The church of the savvy took him at his word, and assumed the worst.

Turns out they were right. But that doesn’t mean they should be proud of it.

That dog, it turned out, didn’t just not hunt — it was never even let out of the house.

raw_text:
David Gregory: No, I won’t fact check my guests and you guys can’t make me. (A Time Line)

Lately, David Gregory has been taken to task for his new policy on Meet the Press of letting his guests make false statements without any challenge or fact checking. When asked, he said it was the job of other people, not him, to fact check his guests.

I’ve been watching this happen for months. It started to be really noticeable in late 2009. But when I went back and looked at the record, I saw that it really started not long after he took over Meet the Press.

In case you are interested, here is a time line of David Gregory’s performance on Meet the Press as it relates to his fact checking the statements of his guests.

September 2008: Tim Russert dies, Tom Brokaw takes over Meet the Press temporarily. Gregory is named as the permanent host in December 2008.

January 2009: Gregory interviews Andrew Card, who famously said “From a marketing point of view, you don’t introduce new products in August”. Card lies about the statement and Gregory does not challenge him.

Media Matters: On the January 4 edition of NBC’s Meet the Press, host David Gregory failed to challenge former Bush White House chief of staff Andrew Card’s false claim that he was “misquoted” as saying, “From a marketing point of view, you don’t introduce new products in August.” In fact, Card was quoted as saying precisely that in a September 7, 2002, New York Times article.

July 2009: Gregory lets Sen. Mitch McConnell lie about judges and the SCOTUS.

News Hounds: On Meet The Press today (7/12/09), Republican Senator Mitch McConnell was allowed to get away with a whopper of a lie. David Gregory either didn’t know it was a lie or chose to ignore it. Either way, it’s a major journalistic failure on his part and a huge disservice to the Meet The Press viewers who may not have known better.

August 2009: Gregory has Sen. Orrin Hatch on the show who brings a chart that is full of false information. Gregory not only does not challenge him, but has the chart displayed for all to see.

Media Matters: Hatch displays misleading chart to attack public option.

September 2009: Gregory lets Former New York Gov. George Pataki lie about health care.

Media Matters: During the September 6 edition of NBC’s Meet the Press, host David Gregory allowed former New York Gov. George Pataki (R) to falsely claim that Sen. Ted Kennedy (D-MA), in the last major speech of his life, called for passing health care reform “but not now.” In fact, Kennedy reportedly added the words “this year, this time” to his prepared speech.

January 2010: Gregory lets Sen. Mitch McConnell lie again.

Media Matters: On the January 31 edition of NBC’s Meet the Press, host David Gregory allowed Sen. Minority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-KY) to falsely claim that President Obama “lectured” Republicans during the House Republican Conference retreat.

January 2010: Politifact gives Gregory the prize for allowing the “lie of the year” on his show.

Politifact: The claim is a wildly inaccurate, cynical distortion of the health care bill. It plays on public fears about government and personal health care decisions.

February 2010: Sen. Minority Leader Mitch McConnell tells another whopper, this time about the stimulus and the jobs that were created. Gregory does not challenge him.

Media Matters: On the February 21 edition of NBC’s Meet the Press, moderator David Gregory allowed Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell to falsely claim that “not a single Republican” voted for the stimulus bill because Democrats “wouldn’t allow us to offer a single amendment.” In fact, during Senate consideration of the stimulus, several Republican amendments were offered, and three Republicans voted for the final legislation.

March 2010: Gregory lets Sen. Kyl lie about the health care bill.

Media Matters: On the March 21 edition of NBC’s Meet the Press, Gregory allowed Sen. Jon Kyl (R-AZ) to falsely claim that “a majority of the American people is very substantially opposed to this bill,” adding, “It’s about 60-40, depending on the poll.” In fact, a March 19-20 poll conducted by SurveyUSA found that 48 percent of respondents supported the legislation, while 45 percent opposed it.

April 2010: David Gregory has Rep. Michelle Bachmann on his show. She makes so many false statements that it is hard to keep up. Gregory challenges her on none of them.

Media Matters: Gregory stated: “She said some things that are not true, and you can go to our website and we detail what she said and what the facts are.” But when asked by guest Chuck Todd later in the program if he was “ceding the ground” of fact-checker by not challenging Bachmann during the interview, Gregory replied: “No, because I think there are two things. I think my job is not to say, ‘You’re not telling the truth.'”

Here is a partial list of Bachmann’s lies that Gregory let go unchallenged:

1. Stated that over 50% of people will be forced out of their own private health insurance into a government run program.

2. Said that Obama is spending over a trillion dollars a year on stimulus.

3. Claimed that Obama did not live up to his promise to be post partisan.

4. Claimed that ObamaCare will be a disaster.

5. Repeated the lie that the government will be in charge of health care decisions.

6. Repeated the lie that the health care bill will cost trillions of dollars.

7. Claimed that the CBO did not have a chance to score the final health care bill.

April 2010: Gregory is interviewed by Don Imus and defends his no fact check policy.

Mediaite: David Gregory defended his decision not to fact check Rep. Michele Bachmann on Meet The Press this past Sunday. “It’s not my role to debate them,” Gregory said. “My role is to ask the questions.”

April 2010: Gregory is asked about his new policy and says it is not his job to fact check.

Think Progress: It seems to me that viewers of these Sunday shows tune in to learn something about the issues of the day. Gregory seems to be saying that his role is to simply provide a forum for his guests to say whatever they want, and if they happen to say something that isn’t true, it’s up to his other guests to call them on it. In the case of Bachmann, she appeared on the show by herself, so she had nobody to rebut her. Does this mean any solo guest on Meet the Press now has a license to lie?

April 2010: Gregory appears on MSNBC and says it is the job of the Democrats to fact check Republicans on his show.

From the comments on Mediaite: Here’s a novel idea: How about Gregory just asks a follow-up question when one of these liars is on his show? Maybe a question like this: “Senator, you’ve made a serious charge against the President. Where are you getting your facts?” Then when they can’t come up with anything, he can just stare at them with that smug look of his. The viewers will know which person at the table isn’t very bright.

April 2010: Gregory again says it’s not his job to fact check.

Washington Post: “I think there’s a lot of debate about this,” Gregory told me. “There’s the school of thought that you should just be a truth-squad guy. I think that’s a mistake. I think my job is to get to the truth. . . . I don’t want to be the guy who is the pursed-lip schoolmarm who is lecturing people on what’s right or wrong.”

As Jay Rosen said:

“It is not a matter of a pursed-lip schoolmarm lecturing people. It’s a matter of the host of Meet the Press knowing what he’s talking about, and knowing when a guest is trying to get away with something.”

title: What to reject when you’re rejecting the wisdom of crowds: tips for debunkers
author: Jay Rosen
excerpt: Here are some tips for debunkers: reject the idea that all crowds are wise, reject the idea that all decisions made by crowds are wise, reject the idea that crowds are always right, reject the idea that you are always right when you disagree with a crowd, reject the idea that crowds are always wrong, reject the idea that all crowd wisdom is created equal, reject the idea that you can always tell when a crowd is wise, reject the idea that you should always go with the crowd, reject the idea that you should always go against the crowd, and reject the idea that you can’t learn from crowds.
summary: When considering the wisdom of crowds, it's crucial to avoid blanket statements and recognize the nuanced nature of crowd behavior. It's essential to reject the notion that all crowds or their decisions are inherently wise or always wrong. Factors like emotion, misinformation, and groupthink can sway crowds. Individuals shouldn't automatically assume they are correct when disagreeing with a crowd, nor should they always go against the crowd. There are varying types of crowd wisdom, and the ability to discern when a crowd is wise isn't always obvious. Learning from crowds, even "dumb" ones, is possible, and blindly following or rejecting the crowd should be avoided. The key lies in understanding when and what aspects of crowd behavior should be rejected.
